0-4405-1-3.subevent: A double-decker bus operated by Stagecoach South West overturned on the A385 between Totnes and Paignton while traveling from Torquay to Plymouth at about 11:00 BST.
Police reported up to eight people seriously injured, and 37 people were taken to several hospitals in Devon for treatment.
Emergency services closed the road, declared a major incident (later stood down), sent several ambulances and the air ambulance, and a witness described seeing emergency vehicles everywhere.
Uninjured passengers were taken to Paignton bus station for support and to continue their journeys.
The road will remain closed in both directions for several hours for investigation and recovery, said fire service area manager Gerald Taylor.
Police said the bus driver had not been arrested and was assisting with inquiries; Stagecoach South West stated they are assisting the investigation and that safety is their priority.
Jane Viner, chief nurse, thanked all NHS staff who came in on their day off, and MP Sarah Wollaston thanked the emergency services for their efforts.

9-21073-2-1.subevent: The Portuguese Episcopal Conference announced the suspension of public Masses from Jan. 23, citing the extreme gravity of the pandemic.
Portugal has recorded over 609,000 COVID-19 cases and 9,920 deaths as of Jan. 22, amid a surge in deaths.
This is the second time the bishops have suspended public worship; the first was in March 2020 and was eased at the end of May.
The bishops suspended catechesis and other pastoral activities requiring gatherings, and called on priests to livestream Masses.
Earlier in January, the bishops had called for the suspension or postponement of baptisms, confirmations, and marriages.
Funerals may be celebrated according to norms from May 2020 requiring social distancing.
A Lenten retreat for the bishops, scheduled for Feb. 22-26, was canceled.
The Shrine of Our Lady of Fatima will broadcast three Masses and two rosaries daily during the suspension.
Shrine rector Fr. Carlos Cabecinhas said that while it is not the same as physical presence, it is the only way to participate now.

2-35077-7-1.subevent: A new survey by Human Rights Watch found that the lives of LGBTQ+ people in Afghanistan have dramatically worsened under Taliban rule.
The report documented nearly 60 cases of targeted violence against LGBTQ+ people since August 2021.
Heather Barr of Human Rights Watch stated that before the Taliban takeover, LGBTQ+ people had hope for gradual improvement, but that ended on August 15.
The report noted that while homosexuality was already illegal under the previous government, the Taliban vowed to take a hard line against LGBT people, citing sharia law.
J Lester Feder of OutRight Action International reported cases of gang-rape, mob attacks, and family members hunting LGBT Afghans, with no hope of protection, and few options to flee.
A 16-year-old transgender girl, Zeba Gul, described being locked up, beaten, and abused by her family before and after the Taliban takeover.
After the Taliban came to power, Zeba Gul's family threw her out, and she was attacked, raped, and held and beaten by the Taliban.
Faraydoon Fakoori of Paiwand 34 stated that the situation has worsened for gender minorities with increased violence, harassment, and rape.
Zeba Gul commented that the Taliban's return empowered vigilantes and homophobes, making it open season on LGBT people with no fear of punishment.
In 2021, a Taliban spokesperson stated that homosexuals face stoning or being crushed by a wall.

9-21751-1-5.subevent: Clashes broke out Sunday in Jerusalem's Mea Shearim as police attempted to shut down a yeshiva that opened illegally; hundreds surrounded officers, shouting insults and throwing debris, leading to one arrest and water cannon deployment.

In Ashdod, police were confronted while closing an ultra-Orthodox elementary school that opened illegally; dozens tried to force entry, injuring four officers and damaging the fence, and four people were arrested.

In Bnei Brak, clashes occurred as police tried to shut down schools linked to the Vizhnitz Hasidic dynasty, whose head rabbi initially ruled that educational institutions should open but backtracked hours later.
Police said in response to the violence that they would continue to enforce virus restrictions in all communities.
The lockdown, extended to January 31, has shuttered nonessential businesses and the entire education system, but some ultra-Orthodox schools have continued to operate in violation.

Last week, a mob in Bnei Brak injured a police officer, leading to six arrests; Prime Minister Netanyahu condemned the attack, but critics accused him of avoiding a crackdown on the ultra-Orthodox to keep his coalition partners happy.

Additional lockdown violations emerged, including a mass gathering in the Sanz Hasidic sect in Netanya, and other sects are expected to hold prayers and gatherings; Health Minister Yuli Edelstein called for jailing those who broke lockdown rules.

Netanyahu and Edelstein appealed to Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky, who gave permission for some ultra-Orthodox schools to reopen but only if it does not spark a confrontation with police, though some schools were hesitant.

The Health Ministry reported a decline in daily infections, with 2,394 new cases Saturday, while noting that Haredi communities have suffered disproportionately from the coronavirus with higher infection rates.

1-wiki-img/15489-4/15489-4-3.subevent: The New Horizons spacecraft flew by Pluto in July 2015.
Researchers observed a variety of terrains across Pluto, including jagged spikes at high altitudes.
New research found that the blades are made mostly of methane ice and form similarly to Earth's penitentes.
The spikes form at high altitudes where methane freezes directly from gas to solid, and during warmer periods, parts of the methane ice sublimate back to gas.
Jeffrey Moore explained that Pluto's climate variation causes methane ice to evaporate.
On Earth, similar structures called penitentes are only a few meters tall and form at high altitudes near the equator.
Slight irregularities in snow lead to longer spikes due to differential sublimation.
The presence of penitentes on Pluto helps researchers understand surface temperature changes and map topography.
The new study will be published in the journal Icarus.

0-4766-1-3.subevent: A South West Aviation Let L-410, registration UR-TWO, crashed into Yirol Lake near Yirol City while on approach, killing 20 people and leaving 3 survivors.
Initial rescue efforts by local fishermen recovered 19 bodies, and 4 survivors were taken to a hospital with serious injuries.
On Sep 10 2018, authorities reported that 20 people had died and 3 survived, and Eastern Lake State declared three days of national mourning.
The Aviation Herald received a passenger manifest showing the operator was South West Aviation, listing 17 adults and 3 children, including citizens of Uganda, Ethiopia, and South Sudan.
Italian media reported that an Italian doctor working for an NGO in South Sudan was among the survivors and was taken to Juba with serious injuries.
The aircraft, MSN 841328, had been previously operated by Universal-Avia and later owned by SlavAir, with tail number UR-TWO assigned on Apr 11 2018.

On Nov 19 2018, Ukraine's NBAAI reported the accident, stating that 20 people were killed and 3 injured, and that they had assigned an accredited representative and read out parametric data from the flight data recorder.

On Oct 23 2019, Ukraine's NBAAI published the final report from South Sudan's Ministry of Transport, concluding probable causes were severe weather, pilot error in setting the altimeter, and replacement of a faulty propeller without informing safety authorities.

5-wiki-img/5789-8/5789-8-2.subevent: A report claims climate change can still be tackled if people embrace major lifestyle shifts, and it provides a list of the best ways to reduce carbon footprints based on an analysis of 7,000 studies.
The report notes that public willingness to accept radical change has been shown by the Covid-19 crisis, and that government priorities must be reordered with protecting the planet as the first duty.

The top recommended action is living car-free (saves 2.04 tonnes CO2e per person annually), followed by driving a battery electric car (1.95 tonnes) and taking one less long-haul flight (1.68 tonnes).
Switching to a vegan diet saves 0.8 tonnes but less than transport, and popular activities like recycling save only 0.01 tonnes and are worthwhile but less effective.

Lead author Dr Diana Ivanova says a complete change of mindset is needed, that the top 10 options are available without expensive new technologies, and that rich people who fly and drive big cars consume the most, calling aviation under-taxed a moral issue.

She ranks other actions: buying renewable power and public transport (4th and 5th), insulating home (6th, 0.895 tonnes), vegan diet (7th, 0.8 tonnes), and other top actions like heat pumps and renewable heating.
Dr Ivanova estimates that implementing these measures would save around 9 tonnes CO2e per person per year, compared to current household emissions of 10 tonnes in the UK and 17 in the US.
The study lists lesser-impact actions: green roofs, using less paper, buying durable items, turning down the thermostat, and recycling.

Some findings are questioned; polls show varying public views. Professor Tommy Wiedmann says the study is valuable but overlooks impacts like water scarcity from lithium mining. Libby Peake says people should keep recycling and that better design can reduce consumption and carbon footprints.

19-28321-12-t.subevent: Muslims accept that capital punishment is a punishment established by God in the Qur'an, and that it is acceptable when required by law despite murder being a sin.
The Prophet Muhammad sentenced people to death for murder, which is a reason Muslims accept the death penalty.
Shari'ah law states that the punishment for murder, adultery, and denying Islam is the death penalty.
Some Muslims argue against capital punishment because although it is allowed in the Qur'an, they do not think it is compulsory.
Shari'ah law allows the family of a murder victim to accept money as reparation instead of enforcing the death penalty.
Some Muslims believe that only Allah has the right to take life, so carrying out the death penalty is 'playing God' and committing shirk.

1-14826-2-3.subevent: Alicia Soto attended the 1 October Sunrise Remembrance Ceremony for the third year to help process her trauma.
Soto said she lost a part of herself that night and decided to live life to the fullest for those who died.
A slideshow displayed the names and pictures of the 58 people killed and two additional women who died within the past year from injuries.
Clark County Sheriff Joe Lombardo announced that Kimberly Gervais and Samanta Arjune will be added to the official death toll, raising it to 60.
The announcement followed a Review-Journal article that highlighted their deaths and Metro's initial decision not to include them.
Lombardo said he is comfortable acknowledging the two individuals lost their lives as a result of 1 October.
The ceremony had fewer attendees due to the pandemic, and Gov. Steve Sisolak prioritized the event.
Sisolak gave a speech with a shaky voice, saying we will never forget what happened.
Albert Rivera, father of victim Jordyn Rivera, thanked survivors, acknowledged Greg Zanis, and called for unity.

1-15289-5-1.subevent: President Joko Widodo requested a suspension of revisions to the Coal and Mineral Mining Law last year, but deliberations resumed under a new working committee of DPR and government members.

The proposed revisions were widely criticized for pandering to the coal mining industry and threatening communities and the environment, and students demanded their rejection in protests across Indonesia in late September 2019.

On 25 September 2019, the Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources submitted a list of 938 concerns, and the DPR abandoned plans to push the revisions through after public pressure and Jokowi's call for delay.
Incoming DPR members (55% returning) resumed discussions, with a working committee agreeing on 235 of 703 proposed changes, while the draft remained unchanged from the previous year.

The revisions ease permit processes, allow companies to extend permits without offering concessions to state-owned firms, remove the 15,000-hectare cap on concession areas, and permit multiple permits per province for the same commodity.
The revisions drop prison terms for officials who approve problematic permits and add fines and prison terms for anyone hindering mining activities, while removing communities' right to veto mining.

The revisions end company responsibility for site rehabilitation, proposing that abandoned pits be used for irrigation or tourism, despite 3,033 pits left unfilled from 2014–2018 causing 140 deaths, and ignore disaster risk reduction, exacerbating floods like Samarinda's 150 flood events from 2009–2014.
The revisions privilege coal as a commodity, conflicting with climate commitments and Indonesia's goal to reduce coal reliance, as coal still constituted 60% of the energy mix in 2018.

1-15091-1-1.subevent: In December 2020, scientists published a paper describing the dinosaur Ubirajara jubatus from a fossil housed in Germany.
Brazilian paleontologists questioned the legality of the fossil's export from Brazil and demanded its return, leading to the temporary withdrawal of the paper on December 24, 2020.
The Baden-Württemberg ministry backed the museum's ownership claim, stating the fossil was legally acquired, which outraged the Brazilian paleontology community.
Cretaceous Research permanently retracted the paper due to unresolved export permission concerns.
The journal updated its policy to reject papers on fossils of uncertain or illegal provenance.
The retraction rekindled Brazilian demands for the fossil's repatriation, and the ministry said it would reexamine the process.
A preprint analysis showed that many paleontology papers involving fossils from developing countries lack local authors, a practice called parachute science.
Some paleontologists argued that fossils are safer in European and U.S. museums, while Brazilian scientists countered that they have adequate infrastructure.
Other researchers voluntarily repatriated Brazilian fossils, including a spider fossil from the University of Kansas.
Scientists noted that the retraction leaves the species nonexistent to science, calling it a second extinction.

1-14990-2-1.subevent: NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope captured enough light from exoplanets to identify molecules in their atmospheres for the first time.
This landmark achievement came years before astronomers anticipated and is a significant step toward detecting life on rocky exoplanets.
Spitzer obtained spectra for two hot Jupiters, HD 209458b and HD 189733b.
The data show the planets are drier and cloudier than predicted, with no water detected and hints of silicates in HD 209458b's atmosphere.
Three teams of astronomers used Spitzer to capture exoplanet spectra, all with similar results.
The secondary eclipse technique was used to isolate the planets' light from their stars.
Previous Hubble observations of HD 209458b revealed individual elements and less sodium than predicted, supporting the presence of high clouds.
Astronomers plan to use Spitzer for further studies of transiting exoplanets and eventually to look for life molecules on rocky planets.

0-4469-10-1.subevent: President Donald Trump’s import tariffs will do more harm than good to the U.S. economy, say the vast majority of economists polled by Reuters.
Nearly 90 percent of 71 respondents said they were concerned tariffs on steel and aluminum imports would lead to a wider trade war, including almost a third who said they were “very concerned.”

Nearly 80 percent of 60 economists who answered a question on the tariffs said they would do more harm than good and the rest said it would do nothing or very little; not one respondent said they would benefit the U.S. economy.

The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development on Tuesday raised its global growth forecasts to the highest since 2011 but warned the world economy was vulnerable to trade tensions after the import tariffs.

The latest poll showed the U.S. central bank will raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points at the March 20-21 meeting and repeat that move three more times, taking the base rate to 2.25-2.50 percent by end-2018.
The Fed’s preferred gauge of inflation, the core PCE price index, was forecast to reach the central bank’s 2 percent target in the third quarter and rise slightly above that next year.
Economic growth forecasts were raised, with full-year median forecasts of 2.8 percent for 2018 and 2.4 percent for 2019.
While most economists said fiscal stimulus from tax cuts and additional spending would benefit the economy this year they were mostly split on if it had brought the next downturn closer.
The median probability of a recession in the coming year was 13 percent, a slight increase from 10 percent in a November poll.

13-23825-1-t.subevent: The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) ruled that Channel 4's poster campaign for Big Fat Gypsy Weddings was irresponsible, offensive, and reinforced negative stereotypes against Gypsy and Traveller communities.
The ASA found that a poster featuring a 15-year-old girl in a low-cut top with visible bra depicted a child in a sexualised way, violating advertising rules.
The ASA also criticized a poster of an aggressive-looking young boy, ruling it endorsed negative stereotypes and could cause distress to Gypsy and Traveller children.
Yvonne MacNamara, chief executive of the Irish Traveller Movement in Britain, condemned Channel 4's 'morally bankrupt' brand.
The Irish Traveller Movement and co-complainants successfully appealed the ASA's initial decision not to investigate the campaign despite nearly 400 complaints.
Channel 4 defended the campaign, stating it was approved at the highest level and submitted to the industry's CAP copy advice team, and apologized for any offence caused.
Channel 4 announced it would not make further series of Big Fat Gypsy Weddings but would produce six 'Gypsy-themed' one-off specials in the next year.
In March, media regulator Ofcom dismissed complaints that the TV campaign breached broadcasting codes.

0-4321-1-1.subevent: A man with a sword-like weapon and a firearm killed one person and wounded at least nine others at a school inside a shopping centre in Finland.
Police used a gun to stop the violence at the Herman shopping centre, which was evacuated.
Police did not confirm that they shot the suspect, who is a Finnish national.
One person died and 10 people, including the suspect and a police officer, were injured, with two victims suffering serious injuries.
Prime minister Antti Rinne tweeted that the violence was 'shocking and totally condemnable'.
The shopping centre houses the Savo Vocational College, where the attacker allegedly entered with some sort of sword, according to Finnish media.

6-18793-1-t.subevent: Matteo Bruni announced on Monday that Pope Francis will visit Iraq, breaking a 15-month hiatus from international travel.
The Pope will make an Apostolic Journey to Iraq, visiting Baghdad, the plain of Ur, Erbil, Mosul, and Qaraqosh over four days in four provinces.
The Vatican said the itinerary will be released later, taking into account the evolution of the worldwide health emergency.
On 10 June 2019, Pope Francis told a meeting of Catholic aid agencies that he planned to travel to Iraq in 2020.
Pope St. John Paul II had planned to travel to Iraq at the end of 1999, but the trip was postponed by Saddam Hussein.
Cardinal Louis Raphael Sako said that Pope Francis will receive an enthusiastic welcome in Iraq.
On 25 January, Pope Francis met with Iraqi President Barham Salih at the Vatican and discussed preserving the historical presence of Christians in Iraq and ensuring their security.
UNICEF estimates that about 4 million Iraqis require humanitarian assistance, half of whom are children.
Cardinal Sako said that Pope Francis' visit will bring a breath of fresh hope to Iraq.

8-6204-1-5.subevent: Two people died in the bushfires on Kangaroo Island, as announced by authorities.
South Australian Premier Steven Marshall stated that forensic police are en route and expressed condolences.
The Southern Ocean Lodge was completely destroyed by the fire, and the operators plan to rebuild.
Most emergency-level fires on Kangaroo Island eased overnight, but one fire on the western half remained uncontrolled.
Mayor Michael Pengilly reported that half of the island was burned, with immense destruction and expected losses of livestock and property.
The South Australian Country Fire Service issued an extreme fire danger warning and urged non-essential travel to the island to be deferred.
Mainland South Australia experienced smoke and dust, and the Chief Public Health Officer advised people with respiratory conditions to stay indoors.
The article noted that Victoria and New South Wales were bracing for catastrophic conditions.

0-4480-4-t.subevent: Two years after the antisemitic attack on the synagogue in Halle, memorial vigils and rallies are taking place in the city.
Saxony-Anhalt's Minister President Haseloff calls for civil courage and warns against a coarsening of language.

Several hundred people in Halle observe moments of silence on Saturday afternoon to commemorate the victims of the terrorist attack of October 9, 2019, and life on the market square comes to a standstill.
In memory of the victims and the bereaved, actions, vigils, and rallies are planned in the city until the evening.

0-4299-6-4.subevent: Ukraine's government and pro-Russia rebels agreed a memorandum at Minsk talks, including a 30km buffer zone, ban on overflights, and withdrawal of foreign mercenaries.
More than 3,000 people have died in fighting since April, and the original ceasefire is still holding despite frequent violations.
Ukraine accuses Russia of arming separatists and sending troops, but Russia denies any involvement.
Three powerful blasts rocked Donetsk, possibly hitting a chemical plant, while a Russian humanitarian convoy of 200 lorries arrived without Ukraine's authorization.
The deal was reached after late-night talks; Leonid Kuchma said heavy weapons would be moved 15km from the front line within 24 hours with OSCE monitoring.
Separatist leader Alexander Zakharchenko said the status of rebel-held areas was not discussed.
Ukraine's parliament passed a bill granting three-year self-rule to parts of Donetsk and Luhansk, which some lawmakers called capitulation.
Russian ambassador Mikhail Zurabov said mercenaries are fighting on both sides and called on the OSCE to oversee their removal.
There are fears in Ukraine that Russia wants to create a frozen conflict in eastern Ukraine.

1-14897-1-2.subevent: Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon rose more than 50% in the first three months of 2020 compared to the same period in 2019, according to satellite data.

Scientists warned that Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro's development-friendly policies could transform the Amazon into a drier savannah, potentially turning it from a carbon sink into a source of emissions.
Since the COVID-19 outbreak, Brazil's environmental agency scaled back enforcement measures, leaving the forest and indigenous tribes more vulnerable.
Indigenous leaders reported continued invasions by loggers and hunters and expressed fears that the virus could devastate their communities.
Since taking office in 2019, Bolsonaro slashed funding and enforcement at FUNAI, the indigenous affairs agency, and appointed a federal police officer with agribusiness connections to head it.

In April 2020, FUNAI passed law IN 09, which prevents undemarcated indigenous lands from being labeled as indigenous in the land registry, and another rule, MP 910, was proposed to allow illegal occupants of federal lands to purchase them at reduced prices.

Reports of illegal logging and violent attacks on indigenous reserves increased, including the death of a 15-year-old Yanomami boy from COVID-19 after miners invaded, a complaint by the Karipuna tribe about clearing inside their reserve, and the assassinations of a Uru-eu-wau-wau leader and a Guajajara teacher.
Erival Guajajara of the Guajajara tribe stated, 'We are afraid for our lives because of our vulnerability.'

32-wiki-img/2081-1/2081-1-2.subevent: Washington has become the first US state to legalise human composting, with Governor Jay Inslee signing the bill into law on Tuesday.
Under the new law, people can choose to have their body turned into soil after death, an alternative to cremations and burials that is practical in cities with scarce land for graveyards.
At the end of the composting process, loved ones are given the soil, which they can use in planting flowers, vegetables, or trees.

Katrina Spade, who lobbied for the law, founded a company called Recompose that could be the first to provide the service, and she stated that recomposition offers a natural, safe, sustainable alternative with significant savings in carbon emissions and land usage.
The process places a body in a hexagonal steel container filled with alfalfa, wood chips and straw, where it decomposes naturally within 30 days, creating two wheelbarrows' worth of soil.
Environmentally friendly burial alternatives are becoming increasingly popular, as illustrated by late actor Luke Perry being laid to rest in a 'mushroom suit' in California.
The mushroom suit, created by Jae Rhim Lee, reduces the amount of toxic pollutants released into the environment during the body's decomposition and cremation.
The process of human composting is already legal in Sweden, while natural burials without a casket or with a biodegradable coffin are legal in the UK.

3-17461-8-t.subevent: An Iran-linked hacking group attempted to break into U.S. President Donald Trump's re-election campaign but was unsuccessful.
Microsoft reported significant cyber activity by the group targeting current and former U.S. government officials, journalists, and prominent Iranians.
The Trump campaign's director of communications said they had no indication any campaign infrastructure was targeted.
The group made over 2,700 attempts to identify consumer email accounts and attacked 241, with four compromised but not associated with the presidential campaign or U.S. officials.
Tensions between the U.S. and Iran have risen since Trump withdrew from the nuclear accord and reinstated sanctions; Iran gave no immediate comment.
Microsoft said the attacks used personal information to game password reset features, were not technically sophisticated, and the group has been tracked since 2013.

Big tech companies met with U.S. intelligence agencies in September to discuss security strategies for upcoming elections, and Microsoft earlier reported about 10,000 customers targeted by nation-state attacks from Iran, North Korea, and Russia.

17-27607-1-t.subevent: The French rugby federation (FFR) voted unanimously to allow transgender women to play women's rugby as of next season.
The decision goes against World Rugby's advice, which last year said it did not recommend transgender women play women's contact rugby on safety grounds at the international level.
World Rugby's advice was not binding and allowed national federations to implement their own grassroots policy.
FFR Vice President Serge Simon said rugby is an inclusive sport without distinction and that the FFR is against all forms of discrimination.

FFR's statement clarified that transgender women must certify they have been on hormonal treatment for at least 12 months and must not exceed a testosterone threshold of five nanomoles per liter to compete domestically.
Players who have already transitioned and changed their civil record can play without preconditions.
The FFR is the first national federation in France to allow transgender women to compete in top level sport.

0-4763-2-1.subevent: Flight JT610 lost contact 13 minutes after takeoff and crashed into the sea; pilots had asked to turn back.
Flight data showed the plane descended and veered left shortly after takeoff, then climbed and increased speed before data loss.
The jet had a technical issue on a previous flight but was resolved according to procedure.
Safety experts said the top priority will be finding the cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder.
Lion Air's only prior fatal accident was in 2004, but several other jets were damaged beyond repair.
A consultant said Indonesia has a 'chequered past' in air safety and needs improvement.
This is the first crash of a Boeing 737 MAX, introduced last year.
Boeing and the NTSB are assisting in the investigation.
Operators including Lion Air have no plans to remove 737 MAX jets from service; the crashed jet was delivered in August with 800 flight hours.

11-22768-2-1.subevent: Twitter permanently banned conservative writer Milo Yiannopoulos on Tuesday night after he incited racist abuse against Leslie Jones.
Twitter stated Yiannopoulos' ban was for violating rules against inciting targeted abuse and that his account would not be restored.
Twitter does not disclose specific guidelines for permanent bans and generally does not comment on individual accounts.
The article notes a caveat that permanent bans can be mistaken for temporary suspensions, and in three of the five listed cases, banned users provided screenshots.
Charles C. Johnson was permanently banned for publishing personal information and inciting harassment.
In 2015, Twitter permanently banned a man who repeatedly threatened to kill trans people.
A pro-Trump troll was permanently banned after tweeting that a journalist who died of a heart attack had 'killed himself' as a result of his work.
Azealia Banks was indefinitely suspended after homophobic rants targeting Zayn Malik and Skai Jackson; her attempt to return was also blocked.
Twitter said it is continuing to improve its enforcement systems and promised changes to its reporting system and harassment policies.

1-15201-2-2.subevent: Hundreds of church services and other religious ceremonies have been cancelled this weekend in response to the coronavirus crisis.
The Church in Wales suspended all public gatherings, including Mothering Sunday services, earlier this week.
Archbishop of Wales John Davies said prayers could be shared online, with some services being streamed, and that churches are being encouraged to stay open during the day to offer space for prayer.
Archbishop John Davies urged young people whose plans have been disrupted to use their time to help others.
The Catholic church suspended gatherings for public acts of worship as of Friday, after UK government advice.
Archbishop of Cardiff George Stack called for support in heart-breaking times.
The Muslim Council of Britain released guidance calling for suspension of all congregational activities in UK mosques, affecting Friday prayers.
The United Synagogue in the UK said religious gatherings should not go ahead.

5-wiki-img/5817-1/5817-1-1.subevent: China warned that trade talks will be void if US imposes sanctions; after talks with Liu He, China said it was ready to boost imports and released a statement on implementing a previous agreement.
The US threatened to impose extra tariffs on $50bn of Chinese goods.
G7 nations criticized the US over its new steel and aluminum tariffs, and French minister Bruno Le Maire warned a trade war could begin soon.
President Trump tweeted that the US had been ripped off and defended steel tariffs as vital to national security.
China's state news agency Xinhua warned against a trade war and said that if the US introduces trade sanctions, all negotiated achievements will be void.
The White House statement warned of 25% tariffs on $50bn of Chinese imports; analysts said it could be a bargaining tactic.
No joint statement was issued after the Beijing meeting, and there was no US response to Chinese comments.

At the G7 meeting, EU and Canada threatened to retaliate against US steel and aluminum tariffs; US Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin denied the US had abandoned leadership; no joint statement was issued; EU released a list of tariffs on US goods and Canada planned tariffs on US exports.

27-33606-1-1.subevent: Social workers and mental health experts in Fiji called for more tender loving care to address the mental health crisis, especially targeting vulnerable populations during the Covid-19 pandemic.
Lifeline Fiji released suicide statistics for January to July 2021 showing 47 suicides and 65 attempted suicides.
Fiji's Health Ministry recorded 72 suicides in 2020, down from 89 in the same period in 2019.

Fiji Council of Social Services director Vani Catanasiga urged that suicide data from different agencies be made available centrally to enable a more strategic response, and said mental health support needs to be increased.
Mental health specialist Selina Kuruleca agreed, stating that the pandemic has turned into a mental health epidemic and pleaded with the government to listen to suffering people.
Kuruleca said people need to be heard and reassured that the government cares, and that the government is responsible for the welfare of its people.
Kuruleca noted that life in poverty-stricken communities had worsened during the pandemic, with many people living in crowded conditions and requiring more than just food assistance.
On Tuesday, 118 new Covid-19 cases were reported in the community, and one death was confirmed: a 59-year-old man who died after 28 days in hospital.

Health Secretary James Fong reported four additional deaths of Covid-positive patients classified due to pre-existing conditions, and gave current hospitalizations: 114 patients, with two severe and two critical.
Dr. Fong reported 113 new recoveries, bringing active cases to 12,948, total cases to 50,198 since March 2020, and death toll to 576.

0-4389-1-1.subevent: Alejandro Meran stole a scooter and then called his brother for advice.
The brother alerted the police, and both were brought to the Questura.
While at the Questura, Alejandro asked to go to the bathroom, then suddenly grabbed two guns from the officers and shot them point-blank.
He shot one officer, then encountered a second officer and shot him, taking his gun.
He had a shootout with a guard officer, who wounded him.
He fled outside but was stopped by the mobile squad and wounded further.
The brother Carlysle hid in the basement and was uninvolved.
Witnesses heard several shots and saw the suspect try to open a police car; the area was cordoned off.
President Mattarella expressed condolences, the mayor declared city mourning, and the interior minister and police chief arrived in Trieste.

1-16058-7-1.subevent: South Africa and India renewed their bid to waive WTO TRIPS rules to allow generic or other manufacturers to make more vaccines.
South Africa argued the current TRIPS system failed during the HIV/AIDS pandemic, costing at least 11 million African lives.
Médecins Sans Frontières put together a letter signed by over 375 civil society organizations supporting the waiver.
The proposal was backed by dozens of developing countries but opposed by Western countries including Britain, Switzerland, EU nations, and the United States.
India is a major manufacturer of generics, although many of the largest generic companies are based in Western and developed countries.
Western nations argued that protecting intellectual property rights encourages research and innovation and that suspending them would not result in a sudden surge of vaccine supply.
The WTO's TRIPS Council debated for three hours but failed to agree; proposals need consensus of all 164 members.
They agreed to discuss the matter twice again in April before the next scheduled TRIPS Council meeting on June 8-9.

WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala called the discussions vitally important and urged governments and businesses to act now to increase production and collaborate with WHO, GAVI, and business associations to find solutions.

1-15076-2-3.subevent: Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon rose more than 50% in the first three months of 2020 compared to the same period in 2019, according to preliminary satellite data from the Brazilian Space Agency.
Scientists warned that President Jair Bolsonaro's development-friendly policies could push the Amazon past a tipping point, causing it to emit more greenhouse gases than it captures.
Brazil's environmental agency scaled back enforcement measures during the COVID-19 pandemic, increasing the vulnerability of indigenous tribes to illegal logging and mining.
Indigenous leaders reported continued invasions of their territories and expressed fear that the coronavirus could spread to their communities.

The Bolsonaro administration slashed funding for the indigenous affairs agency FUNAI and passed controversial legislation, including IN 09 and MP 910, which critics say facilitates land grabbing; the administration denied the rules would legitimize land grabbing.

Since the enforcement rollbacks, reports of illegal logging and violent attacks increased, including the death of a 15-year-old Yanomami boy from COVID-19 linked to illegal miners and the assassinations of indigenous leaders in April and March.
The Guajajara tribe's 'Guardians' previously conducted patrols against illegal loggers, as documented in the film 'Guardians of the Amazon.'

1-14879-3-t.subevent: Police fired tear gas at protesters at a religious festival in Bishoftu, triggering a stampede that killed 52 people, according to the regional government.
The regional government blamed 'irresponsible forces' for the violence, while opposition groups claimed the death toll exceeded 100.
Some festival participants crossed their wrists above their heads, a gesture that has become a symbol of protest by the Oromo community.
Protesters threw stones and bottles, and security forces responded with baton charges and tear gas; there were some reports of gunfire.
The police action sent people fleeing in panic, with many falling into a ditch; police demanded that an AFP photographer leave the scene.
Oromo activists called for 'five days of rage' to protest the deaths, and a strong police presence was visible.

Protester Mohamed Jafar accused the government of being a dictatorship controlled by the Tigrayan People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that overthrew Mengistu in 1991 and is accused of monopolizing power.
The annual Irreecha festival is celebrated by millions on the shores of Lake Harsadi; anti-government protests began in the Oromo region in 2015 and later spread to the Amhara region.

Protester Habte Bulcha said the Oromo people have been marginalized for 25 years, and together Oromos and Amharas make up 60% of the population, rejecting the disproportionate power of the Tigrean minority.

9-20978-5-t.subevent: Dr. Jennifer McCormick, Indiana's State Superintendent of Public Instruction, announced that all K-12 schools in Indiana will remain closed through the end of the school year and must provide instruction via remote learning.
Schools will not conduct in-person instruction for the remainder of the 2019-2020 school year.
McCormick said the state is reviewing the required number of instructional days; schools previously received a 20-day waiver reducing the requirement to 160 days.

Schools must provide e-learning until they complete 160 instructional days or at least 20 additional days of remote learning between April 2 and the end of the school year; the Indiana Department of Education will waive any remaining difference.
Schools are required to submit a continuous learning plan by April 17.
McCormick said the department will provide guidelines for the plans and that the plans should signal to families, students, and policymakers what instruction is happening.
McCormick said all high school seniors on track to graduate before schools closed on March 19 will be granted flexibility to earn an Indiana diploma.
Indianapolis Public Schools Superintendent Aleesia Johnson expressed support for the decision and said the district will continue serving students and families.

1-15076-2-1.subevent: Deforestation in Brazilian Amazon rose more than 50% in first three months of 2020 compared to the same period in 2019.
Scientists warned that Bolsonaro's policies could cause the Amazon to cross a tipping point and emit more greenhouse gases than it captures.
Brazil's environmental agency scaled back enforcement measures during the COVID-19 pandemic, leaving the forest and indigenous tribes more vulnerable.
Indigenous leaders reported continued invasions; Laercio Guajajara stated that there were still a lot of invasions on their territory.
Andre Karipuna expressed fear that just one infected person could rapidly pass the virus to the whole tribe.
Since taking office in 2019, President Bolsonaro slashed funding and enforcement at FUNAI and appointed a police officer with agribusiness ties to head the agency.

In April 2020, FUNAI passed law IN 09, preventing indigenous lands awaiting demarcation from being labelled indigenous, and MP 910 allows illegal deforesters to purchase protected lands at reduced prices.
The Bolsonaro administration denied that the new land ownership rules facilitate land grabbing, arguing that new landowners will be required to preserve up to 80% of their land.
During the pandemic, illegal gold mining increased in the Yanomami reserve, the Karipuna tribe submitted a complaint about clearing, and two indigenous leaders were killed in March and April.

9-20832-1-t.subevent: The proposed collective bargaining agreement includes a 47% share of annual revenue for players in 2020, increasing to at least 48% in 2021, with a media kicker that could raise the share to 48.5% in seasons with 17 games.

Minimum salaries for rookies increase by $100,000 in 2020, with further increases, and other minimum salaried players see at least $90,000 increases in 2020, plus additional benefits like a new four-year player benefit and bonus payments for 17-game seasons.
Performance-based pay rises to $8.5 million in 2020 and $10 million in 2021, average minimum team cash spending increases to 90% over periods, and tenders for restricted free agents increase.
Practice squad size increases to 14 players with higher weekly pay, fifth-year options become fully guaranteed, and pay for all offseason activities increases.
Training camp includes a five-day acclimation period, a 2.5-hour limit on padded practices, limits on consecutive padded days, and a three-day weekend at the end of camp if 17 games are implemented.

Working conditions improve with mandated upgrades to visiting team locker rooms, standards for rehabilitation facilities, an increase in active squad by one offensive lineman, and development of improved field safety metrics.

Benefit increases for active players include a 10% pension increase, higher 401k matching, annuity increases, tuition reimbursement, and improved injury protection, while former players receive a retroactive pension increase, expanded eligibility, and a new hospital network for care.

The drug policy narrows the THC testing window to two weeks at the start of training camp, reduces penalties and eliminates game suspensions for positive tests, and increases the nanogram limit from 35 to 150.

Other changes include clear parameters for player data ownership, reduction in on-field and club fines, implementation of a neutral decision-maker for most Commissioner discipline cases, a 34-week pay period option, and a new workers comp process.

26-13829-1-6.subevent: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, in a pre-recorded address to an online climate conference hosted by Japan, urged Japan and other wealthy nations to abandon reliance on coal and fossil fuels and invest in green energy as part of pandemic recovery.

Guterres noted that many countries are using the pandemic to double down on green energy to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, and said the world faces two critical crises, expressing hope the meeting would be a turning point.
The major UN Climate Change Conference (COP26) was postponed from November 2020 to November 2021 due to the pandemic.
Japan's Environment Ministry launched the Platform for Redesign 2020 to collate countries' climate policies in pandemic recovery.

Guterres said Japan should lead in renewable energy and stop financing coal plants, and listed priorities including green jobs, ending fossil fuel subsidies, and integrating climate into decisions, arguing clean energy brings economic benefits and coal plants are stranded assets.
Japan scaled back its renewable ambitions after the 2011 disasters, closed most nuclear plants, boosted coal, oil, gas, and solar, and also financed coal plants abroad.
Guterres said the goals of halving emissions by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2050 are achievable but off track, and urged ambitious plans before COP26.
Japan's Environment Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said the platform aims to help countries redesign systems during dual crises, and that the task is to build back better.

4-35504-1-1.subevent: UNESCO re-elected Audrey Azoulay as director-general for a second mandate with 155 votes in favor, nine against, and one abstention.
Azoulay said the result is a sign of regained unity and restored confidence in UNESCO.
Azoulay said she reduced political tensions and found common positions on divisive subjects.
UNESCO has been involved in projects such as rebuilding the old city of Mosul and schools in Beirut damaged by a 2020 blast.
Azoulay's greatest challenge for her second term is to woo Israel and the US back into UNESCO.
A source close to Azoulay said there were positive signs that Israel and the US could consider returning.
The return of the US could balance China's growing influence and mandatory budget contributions.

22-wiki-img/3456-2/3456-2-3.subevent: President Donald Trump discussed buying Greenland for the United States with aides and allies.
A Trump ally said the president was not serious about the purchase.
A Republican congressional aide said Trump brought up the notion multiple times but lawmakers did not take his comments seriously.
Greenland's government stated that the island is not for sale.
In 1946, the United States proposed to pay Denmark $100 million to purchase Greenland.
Neither the White House nor Denmark commented on the reports.
Trump is scheduled to visit Denmark next month.

4-35464-1-1.subevent: Estonia assessed the risk of becoming a transit channel for illegal immigrants heading to Nordic countries, and five illegal immigrants from Belarus were caught, with two sent back to Iraq, one to be sent back, and one sent to Russia, while proceedings for two others continue.
Police focus on EU internal borders, especially the Tallinn passenger port.

Defense Minister Laanet said migrants cause issues in Belarus, Iraqi authorities prepare return flights but migrants not interested, and Baltic defense ministers expressed support for Poland, with Estonia willing to assist.
Interior Minister Jaani said Poland hasn't called for help, but Estonia is prepared to help through the EU and directly.
Construction of the Estonian-Russian border fence progressed well, with 23 km in high-risk areas and 63 km under construction.
The Police and Border Guard Board started negotiations to speed up construction and brought forward procurements; the ministry has agreements for temporary barriers.

Prime Minister Kallas said Estonia is deeply concerned about the situation on the Polish-Belarusian border and supports Poland, raising the issue in the UN Security Council, and she communicated with the Polish prime minister.
Kallas said the European Commission president called it a hybrid attack and the European Council president said physical funding for the EU external border should come from the EU budget.
A decision on supplementary sanctions against Belarus is expected at the EU Foreign Affairs Council on Monday.

2-34872-1-1.subevent: Sri Lanka re-opened schools for primary students on Monday after almost five months.
The Education Ministry said students are permitted to attend school in suitable attire from Monday.

Education Secretary Professor Kapila Perera explained the decision was reached because many students could not source school material and uniforms given the present situation, and emphasized that attending school is most important.
Sri Lanka’s health sector called on education authorities and parents to ensure all necessary health guidelines are followed.
Director-General of Health Services Dr. Asela Gunawardena told News 1st that parents must refrain from sending their children to school if they are ill or have a fever.

0-4745-1-3.subevent: Emperor Naruhito officially proclaimed his enthronement in the centuries-old Sokui no Rei ceremony at the Imperial Palace in Tokyo.
Purple curtains were pulled back to reveal Naruhito and Empress Masako sitting on thrones, wearing traditional robes, while Prince Hitachi watched from a wheelchair.

Naruhito read a proclamation pledging to act according to the Constitution and fulfill his responsibility as the symbol of the state, and expressed hope for Japan's development and international peace.
Prime Minister Shinzo Abe read a speech, bowed, and yelled 'Long live the emperor!'
Boxes believed to contain the sacred sword and jewel, part of the imperial regalia, were placed next to Naruhito.
Naruhito received felicitations from representatives and prayed at Shinto shrines, with high-profile guests including Prince Charles, Carrie Lam, and South Korea's Prime Minister attending.
The enthronement ceremony will be followed by an imperial banquet on Tuesday night.
Due to the devastation from Typhoon Hagibis, a public parade was postponed to November, and the government announced the pardon of about 550,000 petty criminals.

Naruhito became the 126th Emperor of Japan in May, starting the Reiwa era, and the role of the emperor is now symbolic with no political power, while he pledged to continue his father's legacy of breaking down barriers.

0-4775-3-1.subevent: The High Court observed that journalists digging out information and publishing it is not an offence, while hearing a bail petition filed by Moazzem Hossain.
Moazzem's lawyer, Murad Reza, argued that a journalist had collected the video clip from Moazzem's phone and spread it on social media.
The HC refused to grant bail to Moazzem due to the specific allegation that he recorded and circulated Nusrat's statement without permission.
The HC kept the bail petition stand over for the next three months.
Moazzem has been in jail since June 16, 2019.
On November 29, 2019, a Dhaka court sentenced Moazzem to eight years' rigorous imprisonment for the offence.
Nusrat Jahan Rafi was set on fire on April 6, 2019, allegedly for refusing to withdraw a sexual assault case, and she died five days later.

4-35263-4-1.subevent: Saudi Arabia announced that the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah will gradually open to the public starting Sunday.

Saudi Arabia also announced that mosques across the Kingdom, except those in Makkah, will open their doors to worshippers on Sunday as part of easing curfew restrictions to prevent the spread of COVID-19.

The Saudi minister of Islamic affairs announced on Friday the readiness of the Kingdom's mosques to welcome worshippers after completing field trips, stating that they had completed preparations and were in the best condition.

6-20152-2-1.subevent: The federal government announced an easing of cross-border travel policies to allow more extended family members into Canada on compassionate grounds.
As of Oct. 8, extended family members including those in exclusive dating relationships for at least one year, adult children, grandchildren, siblings, and grandparents can enter Canada.
Also as of Oct. 8, non-relative foreign nationals under compassionate reasons such as a close friend with a life-threatening illness can enter Canada.
As of Oct. 20, international students attending institutions with approved COVID-19 readiness plans can enter Canada.
The government will deploy 190 public health officers and enhance monitoring, including digital portals for traveller information.
Travellers entering Canada must still quarantine for 14 days and pass a health check before boarding.
Prime Minister Trudeau stated that community transmission is the main driver of COVID-19 cases and travel cases are a tiny fraction.
Conservative immigration critic Raquel Dancho said the policy change is welcome but late for some.

0-4346-1-t.subevent: The United States announced 10% tariffs on European-made Airbus planes and 25% duties on French wine, Scotch and Irish whiskies, and cheese from across Europe as punishment for illegal EU aircraft subsidies.
The World Trade Organization authorized the United States to impose tariffs on $7.5 billion worth of EU goods annually in the long-running aircraft subsidies case.
The U.S. tariff list includes large Airbus planes made in France, Britain, Germany and Spain, but exempts EU-made aircraft parts used in Airbus' Alabama assembly operations and those used by Boeing.
U.S. Trade Representative Robert Lighthizer said the WTO confirmed the U.S. is entitled to impose countermeasures and that the U.S. expects to enter negotiations with the EU.
The tariffs target Spanish olives, British sweaters and woollens, German tools and coffee, British whisky, French wine, and cheese from nearly every EU country, but spare Italian wine and olive oil.
The size and scope of the tariffs were reduced from a $25 billion list floated earlier this year, and the USTR warned it can increase the tariffs at any time.
The USTR sought WTO ratification of its tariff list by Oct. 14, with duties possibly coming into force three days after a scheduled tariff increase on Chinese goods.
Airbus spokesman Clay McConnell said the company was evaluating the list and that the WTO would grant the EU authority to impose tariffs on U.S. goods over Boeing subsidies.
Delta Air Lines said it has about 170 Airbus planes on order that could be affected, warning that tariffs would inflict serious harm on U.S. airlines.

9-21116-1-1.subevent: The Vatican Museums director, Barbara Jatta, stated that the intention is to reopen the Vatican Museums on 1 February.
Jatta explained that the current closure was extended for an extra 15 days, in accordance with decisions by the Governorate of the Holy See and Italian government indications.
Jatta noted that the seven-kilometre itinerary mapped out for small numbers of visitors does not constitute a health problem or a vehicle for infection.
Jatta participated in the Italian virtual conference 'More Museum' focusing on the future of museums after the COVID crisis.
Jatta reported a huge increase in visitors through the website and social media channels like YouTube and Instagram, especially during strict lockdown.
Jatta highlighted the success of an Instagram initiative with the Dicastery of Communication and the popularity of 'Face to Face' videos showing museum work during closure.
Jatta noted an increase in young visitors between 18 and 30 years old, partly due to cheaper ticket options.
Jatta reiterated that activity inside the Vatican Museums never stopped, with restoration, editorial work, research, and maintenance continuing during closures.

9-21087-5-t.subevent: Indiana's superintendent of public instruction announced that all K-12 schools in Indiana will provide instruction via remote learning for the remainder of the 2019-2020 school year and will not conduct in-person instruction.
The state is examining required instructional days; schools previously received a 20-day waiver reducing required days to 160.

Schools must provide e-learning until they complete 160 instructional days or at least 20 additional days of remote learning; the Indiana Department of Education will waive any difference if schools complete 20 days but fall short of 160.
Schools are required to submit a continuous learning plan by April 17.
The department is committed to working with schools to provide guidelines for the plans.
All high school seniors on track to graduate before March 19 will be provided flexibility to earn an Indiana diploma.
Indianapolis Public Schools Superintendent Aleesia Johnson expressed support for the decision.

0-4506-1-1.subevent: Indigenous protesters paralyzed roads and blocked a main highway into Quito on the fifth day of anti-austerity unrest, resulting in 477 arrests.

The Conaie organization, led by Jaime Vargas, said demonstrations would continue until President Moreno withdraws the fuel subsidy elimination, and announced that over 20,000 protesters would arrive in Quito to demand the overturn.
President Moreno stated he would not tolerate disorder nor overturn the fuel price hike, and later reiterated calls for dialogue, pledging resources to help the poor.
Interior Minister Paula Romo reported 477 detentions for vandalism since Thursday, and authorities also rounded up about 20 shopkeepers for illegally raising food prices.
Indigenous and workers' movements again blocked roads on Monday with stones, tires, and burning branches, paralyzing the northern entry to Quito.

Police erected barricades around the presidential palace and closed downtown while Moreno assessed the crisis; two dozen policemen were injured in clashes and a man died when his ambulance could not reach him through barricades.
A state of emergency is in place.

The government is struggling with a large foreign debt and fiscal deficit, relying on a $4.2bn IMF loan conditional on belt-tightening reforms, including ending fuel subsidies, trimming the state workforce, and planning privatizations.

9-21449-4-t.subevent: The United States established diplomatic relations with Uganda in 1962, but post-independence despotism and human rights abuses strained relations.
President Museveni came to power in 1986, and since then Uganda has experienced political stability, economic growth, reduced HIV/AIDS, and stabilization of the north, though challenges persist.
Uganda is a key U.S. strategic partner, contributing to the African Union Mission in Somalia and helping weaken the Lord's Resistance Army with U.S. support.

The United States is Uganda's largest bilateral donor, providing assistance that enhances well-being, funds antiretroviral treatment for over 700,000 Ugandans, and shifts to longer-term development in the north, while promoting governance, health, agriculture, and environmental initiatives.

Since 2011, the United States has provided military advisers to the LRA-affected region and significant resources to support counter-LRA efforts, including bringing leaders to justice and assisting communities.
Uganda is eligible for preferential trade benefits under the African Growth and Opportunity Act, and the United States has committed to signing trade agreements with regional organizations.
U.S. exports to Uganda include machinery and wheat, while imports include coffee and cocoa.
The current U.S. Ambassador to Uganda is Deborah Malac.

11-23170-3-t.subevent: Facebook reached an agreement with the Australian government and will restore news pages in Australia in the coming days.

The Australian government introduced last-minute changes to the proposed news media bargaining code, including taking into account existing commercial agreements, giving one month's notice, and a two-month mediation period before mandatory arbitration.
Facebook expressed satisfaction with the changes, saying they address core concerns and allow commercial deals that recognize value.
Under the bill, if digital platforms and publishers cannot reach a commercial deal, government-appointed arbitrators can decide a final price without a middle-ground option.
Seven West Media signed a letter of intent to provide news content to Facebook, following a similar agreement with Google.

Google previously threatened to remove its search service from Australia but later struck deals with publishers including News Corp; Facebook removed news features from Australia, blocking access and accidentally blocking government pages, causing backlash.

Treasurer Josh Frydenberg communicated with Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg to resolve issues, and Facebook's VP Campbell Brown stated the government clarified that Facebook retains control over whether news appears on its platform.

26-14496-2-t.subevent: The #8 Toyota had a suspected puncture, causing the two Toyotas to run out of sync, but the #7 car established a net lead through quicker pitstops and led the #8 by 40 seconds at the four-hour mark.
Both Rebellion cars lost ground at a steady rate, with the third-placed #1 car in danger of being lapped and the fourth-placed #3 car already lapped.
The #4 ByKolles car spent time in the garage in the third hour with an alternator problem and returned to the track eight laps down.

In LMP2, the #39 Graff Racing Oreca gained the lead but then spun, allowing the #37 Jackie Chan DC Racing Oreca to take the lead before the #32 United Autosports Oreca assumed the lead after four hours.
The #38 JOTA Sport Oreca made progress and ran in the top three, while the #30 Duqueine Oreca passed the polesitter.
In GTE Pro, the #97 Aston Martin took the lead by passing the #71 Ferrari, the #51 Ferrari also passed the #71, and the #95 Aston held fourth.
The #92 Porsche went off-sequence after a puncture, and Porsche struggled to match Aston Martin and Ferrari for pace.

In GTE Am, the #83 AF Corse Ferrari pitted under a Slow Zone to take the lead, after the #98 Aston initially led but dropped to third, and the #90 Aston briefly led before being passed by the #56 Porsche, and then the Slow Zone promoted Collard back to the lead; later, Augusto Farfus took over the #98 to reclaim lost ground.

13-24524-1-1.subevent: Roman Catholic bishops voted on a summary document that decided against overhauling the church’s teaching on gay Catholics.
Pope Francis described the Vatican summit as a way to open broader horizons, rising above conspiracy theories and blinkered viewpoints.
The final document agreed on Saturday night reflects a deep rift between conservative and progressive factions.
The document described same-sex marriage as 'not even remotely analogous' to heterosexual marriage.
The bishops concluded that homosexuals should not be discriminated against but said there were 'absolutely no grounds' for gay marriage.
Pope Francis alluded to the scandal and rumor that plagued the synod.
The ruling will come as a blow to LGBT Catholics hoping for a more inclusive outcome.
Monsignor Krzysztof Charamsa announced he was a gay priest and called for the synod to take up the plight of gays; the Vatican subsequently fired him.
The Pope has not lifted any of the homophobic policies of his predecessors, and proposals to reach out to gay people were scrapped last year.

0-4324-1-1.subevent: Meghan Markle and Prince Harry initiated legal proceedings against the Mail on Sunday and its parent company Associated Newspapers over the publication of a private letter.
The letter, dated August 2018, accused her father of ignoring the pain caused by his media comments.
Schillings, their legal firm, called the publication part of a campaign to publish false and deliberately derogatory stories.
Prince Harry defended his wife against what he called a ruthless campaign by the British tabloid press.
Harry stated there is a human cost to the relentless propaganda, especially when knowingly false and malicious.
Harry noted the double standards in positive coverage during their Africa tour versus vilification during her maternity leave.
Harry expressed fear of history repeating, referencing his mother's death and watching his wife fall victim to similar forces.
The couple will pay for the lawsuit privately and donate any damages to an anti-bullying charity.

22-wiki-img/3685-3/3685-3-2.subevent: Génération Identitaire (GI) stages publicity stunts to reclaim French territory from foreign migrants and posts them online.
GI leader Pierre Larti confronts North African men in Paris, stating opposition to replacement of French values by Islamic ones.
GI is sprouting branches across Europe, viewing the continent as a battleground between European and Islamic culture.
Jean-Yves Le Gallou produces a video titled 'Being European' that receives over 3.2 million views on YouTube.
Fdesouche, a news aggregator chronicling chaos in migrant suburbs, gets about 3 million views per month.
Alain Soral's website Égalité et Réconciliation (E&R) has more readers than Fdesouche, and he is regularly prosecuted for incitement.
Eurosceptic students at Sciences Po set up a club called 'Critique of European Reason' (CRE), creating a Eurosceptic safe space.
CRE members celebrated the Brexit vote by gathering outside the UK embassy to drink champagne and sing God Save the Queen.
Alexandre Devecchio identifies a 'Zemmour generation' of young people who feel let down by the gap between expectations and reality.

1-15208-8-t.subevent: The Obama administration announced a major step forward in medical marijuana research regulations, but the DEA neglected to deschedule marijuana as a Schedule I drug while promising to improve access to researchers.
Scientists initially applauded the DEA's announcement but then heard the details and became disappointed.
The DEA concluded that the best way to satisfy researcher demand is to increase the number of federally authorized marijuana growers.
Researchers stated that the problem is not a lack of marijuana supply but the regulatory hoops to obtain it, such as obtaining a Schedule I license from both federal and state authorities.
Ryan Vandrey reported that his last study took a year and a half to be approved, and any small change requires lengthy reevaluation by the DEA with no time limit on their review.
Vandrey said that real change would come from descheduling marijuana or simplifying the research rules, even while it remains a Schedule I drug.

Vandrey expressed concern that states have legalized marijuana without adequate safety data, while DEA head Chuck Rosenberg cited the lack of adequate safety studies as the reason for not descheduling the drug.
Lawmakers continue to push for legislation to streamline the research approval process, such as a bill introduced by Senator Brian Schatz that would place time limits on agencies' review time.

3-17198-4-t.subevent: Macedonia declared a state of emergency in its border areas at the end of August.
Up to 3,000 refugees arrive in Macedonia daily, mainly from the Middle East, and a similar number cross into Serbia and Hungary, hoping to reach Germany.

In the first seven months of 2015, Germany received almost 200,000 asylum requests, over 40% from the Western Balkans, with almost 30,000 from Albania and a similar number from Kosovo, a massive rise from 2014.
Unlike the 1990s conflict-driven exodus of Kosovars, the current movement is driven by economic prospects, despite Albania being a democratic EU candidate.

Surveys found that economic desperation, youth unemployment of about 60%, and visa restrictions drive Kosovars and Albanians to seek jobs in Germany, with Albania also affected by returnees from Greece and Italy and low wages.

Neither Kosovo nor Albania are on Germany's safe countries of origin list yet, but that is set to change; most asylum applications are doomed, but it takes almost a year before people are ordered to leave.
Almost 20,000 asylum applications from Serbia, Macedonia, and Montenegro, mostly Roma, show that despite the Decade of Roma Inclusion ending, many Roma remain vulnerable.
Roma face loss of informal income, discrimination, and poor housing; they see Germany as attractive with its asylum centres and €140 monthly allowance, though they know they likely won't get asylum.
The plight of Roma is a perennial problem, and as long as they suffer poverty and discrimination, they will continue to seek asylum in Germany.

1-15073-3-t.subevent: Hungary offered to help Romania treat COVID-19 patients by sending a letter from Foreign Minister Peter Szijjarto.
Negotiations between Romania and Hungary on the concrete form of assistance are underway.
Romania is the second-least vaccinated country in the EU with 34% of adults fully vaccinated.
Romanian vaccination committee chief Valeriu Gheorghita said hospitals are overwhelmed by COVID patients and likened the situation to Italy at the start of the pandemic.

Romania's daily COVID-19 cases surged from about 1,000 to over 15,000, it registered over 300 deaths in a single day for the first time, and about 1,500 patients are in ICUs, leading President Klaus Iohannis to call it a catastrophe.
Romanian authorities suspended nonemergency medical treatments for 30 days and asked the EU for help through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism.
A hospital fire in Constanta killed seven people in a COVID-19 ICU, the third such fire revealing severe health infrastructure problems.
Szijjarto said Hungary has capacity to care for Romanian patients, and Hungary itself experienced an uptick in hospitalizations, recording 837 new cases versus Romania's 14,467 on Thursday.

3-17363-6-t.subevent: Biomerieux gave its proprietary formula to the Canadian government for free so its national lab can manufacture test kits.
In March, Canada passed emergency legislation allowing the government and third parties to produce patented goods without consent.
Biomerieux did not respond to questions about similar arrangements with other governments or the revenue impact.
Biomerieux reported a 21.5% increase in sales in the first quarter partly due to demand for reagent.
The Public Health Agency of Canada described the arrangement as a temporary license at no cost, with manufacturing still in development.
Biomerieux's Canadian unit emailed customers in early April saying the move was to clear testing backlogs and would allow more testing, reducing backlogs, and it was boosting its own production.
Biomerieux extraction equipment is widely used in Canada and heavy reliance on one brand contributed to a testing slowdown in late March.
PHAC said the deal is an interim solution because its facilities are not meant for long-term manufacturing.
On Thursday, Canada pledged C$1.1 billion for research and drug or vaccine manufacturing.

13-wiki-img/24048-2/24048-2-2.subevent: Malaysia arrested more than 4,000 people for violating lockdown orders as it entered a harsher phase of its Movement Control Order, with police setting up roadblocks and arresting a man who jumped into the Strait of Malacca.
Senior Minister Datuk Seri Ismail Sabri Yaakob announced the shift to harsh mode at a press conference, urging people to adhere to the order.

Lockdown enforcement varies globally, but Malaysia reports one of the highest arrest rates with 4,189 arrested since March 18 and 1,449 charged, while the Philippines arrested over 20,000 and President Duterte threatened to shoot violators.
Malaysia reported that the lockdown is decreasing the spread of COVID-19, with 3,116 total cases and 50 deaths as of Friday.
Google data showed an 81% decrease in Malaysian citizens' presence at retail and recreation sites compared to about a month earlier.
Authorities cracked down on speech by arresting people for alleged misinformation online, leading journalists to self-censor, and human rights advocates warned of curtailed free expression.

Political turmoil followed Mahathir Mohamad's failed attempt to consolidate power in February, leading to the old ruling party returning to power in March, which economists said will hinder the fight against the virus.
The government announced a $57.3 billion stimulus package called PRIHATIN to address the economic impact of COVID-19, as Malaysia is among the first economies in the region to predict a recession.

0-4553-8-1.subevent: A new analysis reports that ocean temperatures are rising 40 percent faster on average than previously thought.
The U.S. government shutdown remained at a logjam.
Norway disclosed the kidnapping of a tycoon’s wife.
The briefing issued a correction: an earlier version misidentified the home state of a farmer who supports President Trump; the farmer is from Mississippi, not Missouri.

1-15677-2-1.subevent: Portuguese bishops announced the suspension of public Masses from Jan. 23, citing the extreme gravity of the pandemic and a moral imperative for maximum precautions.
Portugal has recorded 609,000 COVID-19 cases and 9,920 deaths as of Jan. 22.
This is the second time the bishops have suspended public worship; the first was in March 2020 and restrictions were eased at the end of May.
The suspension includes catechesis and other pastoral activities requiring gatherings, and priests were called to offer livestreamed Masses.
Earlier in January, the bishops called for the suspension or postponement of baptisms, confirmations, and marriages.
Funerals may be celebrated according to norms issued in May 2020 requiring social distance.
A Lenten retreat for the bishops scheduled for Feb. 22-26 has been canceled.

The Shrine of Our Lady of Fatima announced it will broadcast three Masses and two rosary prayers daily during the suspension, and its rector stated that while it is not the same as physical presence, they want to be with viewers through this difficult moment.

12-7589-1-t.subevent: ARISS received approval from NASA Safety to launch the IORS on SpaceX CRS-20 and stow it on the International Space Station.
ARISS transferred the first IORS flight unit, serial number 1001, to NASA Johnson Space Center for launch on SpaceX CRS-20.

The IORS is a foundational element of the ARISS next generation radio system, consisting of a modified JVCKenwood TM-D710GA transceiver, an AMSAT-developed power supply, and providing higher power radio, enhanced voice repeater, updated APRS, and SSTV capabilities.
This first flight IORS will be installed in the ISS Columbus module.
A second flight unit is expected to launch in 2020 for installation in the Russian Service module.
A total of 4 flight units and 10 total units will be built by the ARISS hardware team.
Future upgrades to the next generation system, including a repaired Ham Video system, L-band repeater, and others, are in various stages of design and development.
ARISS still must complete 92 engineering requirements and a Phase III safety review before the IORS can be unstowed and turned on.

20-11296-3-t.subevent: Ebook Central is introduced as the industry's most intuitive ebook platform for users and librarians.
Ebook Central is described as an all-in-one ebook platform for research, teaching, learning, and simpler administration for libraries.
Because the research process is complex, libraries turn to Ebook Central to avoid switching between platforms.
Ebook Central brings content from virtually every publisher into one unified experience so students and faculty can quickly learn the platform and easily discover and use ebook content.
Simple administration makes Ebook Central ideal for librarians, and its easy-to-use administrative module helps libraries manage their entire acquisition program and gather actionable data.

1-16512-7-t.subevent: Taiwan has legalized same-sex sexual activity, banned anti-LGBT discrimination in workplaces and schools, and permitted individuals to change their genders.
Marriage equality was first proposed by the Executive Yuan in 2003 but stalled due to opposition from cabinet members and conservative lawmakers.
In 2012, legislator Yu Mei-Nu attempted to revive the marriage equality proposal but faced significant push-back at the committee level.
The Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) came to majority power in May 2016 when Tsai Ing-wen was sworn in as Taiwan's first female president.

Tsai Ing-wen voiced support for marriage equality in a 2015 Pride video on her Facebook page, saying, 'I support marriage equality. Every person should be able to look for love freely, and freely seek their own happiness.'
Yu Mei-Nu stated she planned to reintroduce marriage equality to the legislative branch later in 2016, but predicted the legislation would not pass until the end of Tsai's term in 2020.

Kuomintang member Jason Hsu said LGBT equality is a top priority and will come about through cross-party collaboration, adding, 'This is an issue that shouldn't be ideological. It's a sign of a society's progressiveness.'
The legislation would allow same-sex couples to inherit wealth and property as well as access surrogacy parent arrangements.
If Taiwan were to pass the legislation, it would become the first state in Asia to have full marriage equality.

6-19465-1-t.subevent: Hyderabad-based CSIR-Indian Institute of Chemical Technology (IICT) has tied up with pharmaceutical giant Cipla to work on development of anti-viral drugs to contain COVID-19.
Research on anti-viral drugs has been ongoing worldwide, but many molecules with anti-viral properties were not widely marketed due to lack of demand.
CSIR-IICT decided to work on three molecules: remdesivir, favipiravir, and baloxavir.
Cipla urged IICT director S Chandrasekhar to start work on these molecules on an immediate basis.
Cipla would upscale the process based on know-how given by CSIR-IICT.

9-wiki-img/20371-3/20371-3-1.subevent: The Dakota County Attorney's Office announced that three Minneapolis police officers were legally justified in fatally shooting Dolal Idd and will not be charged.

Idd's father Bayle Gelle and activists held a news conference demanding Governor Walz assign the case to the Attorney General for a second review, release all videos, create an independent investigative body, and charge the officers; speakers said Black men and people of color are disproportionately denied justice when killed by police.
Jaylani Hussein said Idd's family asked the governor's office to refer the case to the attorney general early on, but Walz failed to step in.
The governor's office declined to address the criticism, with spokeswoman Claire Lancaster stating the attorney general had not asked for the case.
Attorney General's Office spokesman John Stiles said the office had not been involved and declined to say if it would ask to review the case.
In a 13-page memo, Dakota County Attorney Kathy Keena wrote that Idd disobeyed police orders, attempted to flee in his vehicle, and fired a gun at officers first, and she extended condolences.
During a sting operation, officers blocked Idd's vehicle; Idd fired a gun through his window; officers fired back; Idd died at the scene.

Minneapolis police released body camera footage appearing to show Idd firing first; Chief Medaria Arradondo defended the officers, while activists said the clip was insufficient and demanded all video.

11-23362-12-t.subevent: The University of Akron announced it will discontinue men's cross country, men's golf, and women's tennis at the end of the 2019-20 academic year.

The discontinuation is part of a plan to reduce the University's financial support to the Athletics Department by approximately $4.4 million (23 percent) as part of the overall redesign to emerge from the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.
With the change, the University of Akron will have 17 sports (7 men's and 10 women's) and remain a member of the Mid-American Conference.
The move affects 23 male and 9 female student-athletes.
