Director of Athletics Larry Williams said the decisions are difficult but necessary to align with MAC peers and ensure continued investment in high-demand academic programs.
Williams met via video conference with affected student-athletes and committed to offering full support for those who may choose to transfer to continue their sport.
The announcement was made early to allow student-athletes, coaches, and a graduate assistant time to find new positions.
The University considered factors including program cost, athletics facilities, University and community impacts, and likelihood of success in reaching the decision.

2-35071-13-1.subevent: Poland provided refuge to over 700 Belarusians between 18 August and 18 October, with 399 receiving humanitarian visas, 170 confirmed as international protection applicants, 119 coming via a business program, and 64 allowed entry on a case-by-case basis.
The number of Belarusian applicants for international protection in Poland surged compared to previous years, with an average of only 40 per year from 2017 to 2019.
A study published in June by Statistics Poland estimated over 100,000 Belarusians were in Poland at the end of 2019.

Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya made a second visit to Warsaw, meeting with Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki and presidential chief of staff Krzysztof Szczerski to discuss support.
Tsikhanouskaya appealed to Prime Minister Morawiecki for a law change allowing Belarusians under humanitarian protection to work.
Tsikhanouskaya also met with Warsaw Mayor Rafał Trzaskowski to discuss transferring local self-government experience to Belarusian communities.
She spoke at the College of Europe in Natolin and at the opening of a Polish government-sponsored scholarship program for Belarusian students expelled from universities.
Poland launched a 'Solidarity with Belarus' plan allocating 50 million zloty (€11 million) for victim support programs, job market access, and independent media and NGOs.

Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko accused Poland of wanting to grab former Polish territories, and Russia's foreign ministry condemned Poland's attempts to interfere in Belarus's internal affairs.

1-15145-1-2.subevent: Nationwide protests and labour strikes against a new jobs law in Indonesia continued for a third straight day on Thursday.
The 'omnibus' jobs-creation bill was passed into law on Monday, sparking protests.
In the past two days, nearly 600 people were detained and two students seriously injured, while police used tear gas and water cannon to disperse demonstrators.
On Thursday morning, crowds gathered across major cities on Java, including Jakarta and Bandung, according to local media and video footage shared by a union spokesman.
Protester Maulana Syarif asked that the law be repealed immediately, expressing concern for future generations.
KSPI president Said Iqbal said the strike would continue for a third and final day on Thursday, in conjunction with 32 other trade unions.
The government of President Joko Widodo championed the legislation as key to boosting Indonesia's economy by streamlining regulations, cutting red tape, and attracting more foreign direct investment.
The bill sparked outcry from labour unions, students, and academics, who criticized it for a perceived lack of consultation, expedited passage, and problematic clauses.

5-5720-3-t.subevent: An estimated 9.6 million people were severely food-insecure in Southern Africa at the start of the lean season, including 3.3 million in Malawi and nearly 2.4 million in Zimbabwe in Crisis or Emergency.
Three districts in Zimbabwe and two in Madagascar were classified in Emergency food insecurity (IPC phase 4) due to extreme loss of livelihoods.

There was at least an 80% chance of an El Niño phenomenon between October and December 2018, which could exacerbate the situation with below-average rain and increased risk of African armyworm outbreak.

Humanitarian partners activated phase 2 of the Global Inter-Agency Standard Operating Procedures for Early Action to El Niño/La Niña episodes in six high-risk countries: Eswatini, Lesotho, Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique, and Zimbabwe.

Rising levels of food insecurity increased protection risks, particularly for women and children, including heightened risks of child marriage, gender-based violence, and disruption of antiretroviral therapy.

The number of cholera cases in Southern Africa doubled to over 21,000 by the end of October, with new outbreaks in Zimbabwe, Tanzania, Malawi, and Mozambique; the Zimbabwe outbreak was brought under control and an oral cholera vaccination campaign reached 92% of its target.

Other communicable diseases, including plague and measles in Madagascar, measles in Mauritius, Hepatitis E in Namibia, and Ebola preparedness activities in Angola, Tanzania, and Zambia, continued to impact the region.
Civilians were impacted by violence in Comoros and Mozambique, while an estimated 350,000 Congolese nationals were returned to DRC from Angola starting on 25 September.

Governments and humanitarian partners mobilized targeted assistance for the lean season, but urgent comprehensive action was needed to address root causes of chronic vulnerability and build resilience.

17-27253-2-t.subevent: Pope Francis issues the Apostolic Letter 'Antiquum ministerium' instituting the lay ministry of Catechist.
He notes the ancient origins of the catechist ministry, tracing it back to the New Testament.
He recalls the history of catechists, including saints and martyrs, and their role in evangelization.
He references the Second Vatican Council and subsequent synods that emphasized lay involvement in catechesis.
He decides to institute the ministry of Catechist for lay men and women with suitable formation.
He specifies that the Congregation for Divine Worship will publish the Rite of Institution.
He invites Episcopal Conferences to determine formation and admission criteria.
He addresses Oriental Churches to adopt similar provisions.
He urges bishops to promote this ministry for the growth of their communities.

1-14883-2-2.subevent: The WHO announced a new naming system for Covid-19 variants using Greek letters, labeling the UK variant as Alpha, the South African as Beta, and the Indian as Delta.
The WHO said the new system simplifies discussions and helps remove stigma from variant names.
Earlier, the Indian government criticized the naming of variant B.1.617.2 as the 'Indian variant', though the WHO had not officially used that label.

WHO technical lead Maria Van Kerkhove tweeted that no country should be stigmatized for detecting variants and called for robust surveillance and data sharing, and later said in an interview that Greek letters help the public discuss variants in easy-to-use language.

The Greek letters will refer to both variants of concern and interest, with a full list on the WHO website, and they will not replace scientific names; if more than 24 variants are identified, a new naming system will be announced.
A UK government scientist warned that the country is in the early stages of a third wave driven by the Delta (Indian) variant, which spreads more quickly than the Alpha (UK) variant.
Vietnam detected what appears to be a combination of the UK and Indian variants, described by the health minister as 'very dangerous' and able to spread quickly through the air.

0-4610-1-1.subevent: Fort Worth police officer Aaron Dean was jailed on a murder charge after resigning from the force for the shooting death of Atatiana Jefferson; bond was set at $200,000.
Atatiana Jefferson was shot early Saturday after police responded to a welfare check; bodycam footage showed an officer shouting 'put your hands up' and firing through a window.
Jefferson's family attorney Lee Merritt said the family was relieved Dean was behind bars and wanted vigorous prosecution.

Interim Police Chief Ed Kraus announced Dean was placed on detached duty and stripped of his badge and firearm; Kraus said he intended to terminate Dean but Dean resigned, and he would have fired him for policy violations.
Mayor Betsy Price said Jefferson was unjustly taken and a third-party panel would review the police department; Kraus expected an update on charges.
Dean's resignation letter was released by the police union; the union's executive director said Dean has not yet hired an attorney.
Politicians, including Rep. Marc Veasey and City Councilwoman Kelly Allen Gray, questioned the officer's use of force.
Police said the officer perceived a threat and fired one shot; they released bodycam footage but could not release video from inside the house due to state law.
Police Lt. Brandon O'Neil said the officer did not announce himself before firing and that Jefferson's 8-year-old nephew was in the room; the department has spoken with the family.
The Fort Worth Police Officers Association urged a thorough and transparent investigation.

1-16521-7-1.subevent: Humanitarian agencies in the DRC are providing basic support as the number of internally displaced people reaches 2 million for the first time in nearly three years.
In February 2012, the Congolese army launched operations against armed groups, which retaliated by stepping up violent attacks against civilians.
Barbara Shenstone, Head of OCHA in Kinshasa, warned that the army's operations are creating a boomerang effect, causing civilians to pay a heavy price, and that aid will need to be scaled up.

South Kivu recorded a 35% increase in displaced people to over 856,000 by end March 2012, while North Kivu saw a 10% increase to over 547,000; a recent stand-off between the army and defectors has pushed almost 7,000 people into Rwanda since 29 April.

The RRMP programme, run by OCHA and UNICEF, stepped up its work in both Kivu provinces, providing aid through fairs and traditional distributions, while WFP distributed high-energy biscuits to newly displaced households.

In March, NGOs including Norwegian Refugee Council, Solidarités International, International Rescue Committee, and Italian Foundation distributed aid to over 60,000 displaced households in North and South Kivu through fairs, cash transfers, and direct distributions.
WFP announced it intends to use cash transfers as the primary mechanism for meeting the needs of newly displaced households where feasible.
In late March, WFP, UNHCR, and UNICEF appealed for $4 million to help some 16,000 IDPs in Mitwaba, Katanga.

Funding requirements for DRC in 2012 are $718 million, but only $223 million had been received by 14 May; WFP urgently requires $34 million to continue life-saving food assistance to 1.8 million victims through end of 2012, and aid agencies estimate that more money will be needed if the situation deteriorates.

1-14826-2-7.subevent: Alicia Soto attends the 1 October Sunrise Remembrance Ceremony for the third year and shares her experience of losing a part of herself and deciding to live life to the fullest.
The ceremony displays a slideshow with names and pictures of the 58 killed, plus two women who died in the past year from injuries.
Clark County Sheriff Joe Lombardo announces that Kimberly Gervais and Samanta Arjune will be added to the official death toll, raising it to 60.
Lombardo says he is comfortable acknowledging that the two women died as a result of the October 1 shooting.
The ceremony has fewer attendees due to the coronavirus pandemic, and Gov. Steve Sisolak says it was a priority.
Gov. Sisolak says they will never forget the lives lost and changed.
Albert Rivera, father of victim Jordyn Rivera, thanks survivors and acknowledges Greg Zanis, who built crosses and died in May.
Rivera calls for unity and urges people to remember how they came together after the attack.

13-23819-5-2.subevent: Armed forces opened fire at a reunion ceremony for kidnapped girls in Jangebe, reportedly shooting at least three people.
Frustrated by the length of the ceremony, parents threw stones at government officials.
The 279 girls were kidnapped from their school last Friday and were freed on Tuesday.
The girls were kept in Zamfara state government custody and given medical treatment before the handover ceremony.
UN experts called for urgent rehabilitation for the traumatized pupils.
A mother explained that parents were angry because they wanted to return home before dark due to unsafe roads.
In response to the shootings, the Zamfara state government imposed a dusk-to-dawn curfew in Jangebe and stopped all market activities.
President Muhammadu Buhari declared a no-fly zone and banned all mining activities across the state.
No group claimed responsibility, but the kidnapping is believed to be by criminal gangs, not Boko Haram, and authorities denied paying a ransom.

19-28514-5-1.subevent: Public uproar erupted over the establishment of an LGBT office in Accra, Ghana.
Viral photographs of the office's commissioning and fundraising programme spread online.
The presence of diplomats, including Australian High Commissioner Gregory Andrews, sparked speculation about foreign support for the LGBT group.
The National Coalition for Proper Human Sexual Rights and Family Values demanded the office be shut down.
Executive Secretary Moses Foh-Amoaning argued that LGBT rights are not recognized under Ghana's human rights laws and called for the office's closure and prosecution of those involved.
Foh-Amoaning hinted that his group would petition Parliament for immediate passage of comprehensive legislation to prohibit LGBT activities.
Australia's High Commissioner tweeted that Australia supports human rights and rejects discrimination.
LGBT+ Rights Ghana condemned the demand for closure, asserting its irrevocable right to exist under the Ghanaian constitution.

0-4424-1-10.subevent: Jordan's government reached a pay deal with the teachers union to end a one-month strike, with salaries to rise 35-60% next year.
The strike had threatened a political crisis, and the government began legal steps against the unions after they rejected earlier pay hikes.
King Abdullah ordered the government to reach the wage deal.
The government fears new pay demands from other sectors and pension increases would wreck fiscal reforms.
Dozens of activists celebrated, and the union deputy head called on members to resume teaching.
Tens of thousands of pupils returned to school for the first time since the strike began, which was announced after authorities used tear gas on teachers.

The strike became a protest against the government's failure to deliver economic growth, recalling growing disenchantment that spilled into large street protests in summer 2018, and many parents kept children home out of solidarity.
Economists, teachers, and the IMF commented on the strike's causes and the government's fiscal challenges.

0-4528-3-2.subevent: Royal Marines boarded an oil tanker on its way to Syria, which authorities believed was carrying Iranian crude oil to the Baniyas Refinery in Syria, breaching EU sanctions.
Britain's ambassador in Tehran was summoned by Iran over the incident, and Iran's foreign ministry spokesman said the ambassador was summoned over the 'illegal seizure' of the tanker.
Gibraltar's chief minister Fabian Picardo praised the marines and said Gibraltar port and law enforcement agencies detained the super tanker and its cargo on Thursday morning.
About 30 marines from 42 Commando were flown from the UK to Gibraltar to help seize the tanker in a 'relatively benign operation' without major incident.
Mr Picardo said he had written to the presidents of the European Commission and European Council to give details of the sanctions enforced.
The Baniyas refinery has been subject to EU sanctions since 2014 because it provides financial support to the Syrian government.
A spokesman for Prime Minister Theresa May welcomed the 'firm action' by the Gibraltarian authorities.

0-4748-4-t.subevent: A 174-foot section of the FIU-Sweetwater bridge was lifted from its supports, swung across Southwest 8th Street, and lowered into final position just west of 109th Avenue.
FIU students, faculty, staff, and Sweetwater residents watched the bridge move.
FIU President Mark B. Rosenberg praised the project for building bridges and student safety.
The main span, weighing 950 tons, was built next to Southwest 8th Street using an innovative approach to reduce risks to workers, commuters, and pedestrians and prevent traffic tie-ups.
The move was the largest pedestrian bridge move via Self-Propelled Modular Transportation in U.S. history.
U.S. Representative Mario Diaz-Balart commended the collaboration among local, state, and federal partners and said the project represents creative solutions to transportation challenges.
The $14.2 million bridge is funded by a $19.4 million TIGER grant from the U.S. Department of Transportation, along with other agencies including FIU and the City of Sweetwater.
Sweetwater Mayor Orlando Lopez said the bridge will serve as a visually distinctive gateway and is symbolic of growth and partnership with FIU.
The bridge move began at 5 a.m. and took approximately five hours; construction began in spring 2017 and is expected to be completed in early 2019.

21-30661-5-1.subevent: Aid groups reported that attacks in northern Mozambique have displaced close to 400,000 people during three years of Islamist terrorism.
Armed men attacked Matumba Mussa's home, set it on fire, took his three brothers who were later found dismembered, and Mussa fled to a refugee camp.
Insurgents linked to Islamic State took over Mocímboa da Praia in August.
The UN World Food Program's representative stated that over 366,000 people are displaced and WFP has adjusted its program to provide emergency food.
Borges Nhamire of the Center for Public Integrity said the government needs to do more for displaced civilians and lacks logistics to evacuate people.
In November, insurgents killed scores of people and beheaded more than 50 young men on a football pitch in Muatide village.
In April, militants shot or beheaded 52 young people in Muidumb district after they refused to join them.
Defense Minister Jaime Neto said the military is fighting to eliminate the Islamist threat and asked for patience.
The Islamist attacks began in October 2017 when armed men overran police stations in Mocimboa da Praia, leaving up to 2,000 dead and hundreds of thousands displaced.

21-31053-2-1.subevent: Qatar Olympic Committee launched promotional campaign 'We Are Team Qatar' to support Team Qatar stars ahead of Tokyo 2020 Olympics.
A total of 15 athletes will represent Qatar in seven sports at Tokyo 2020 Olympics, including two female athletes in rowing and athletics.
The Qatari women's representatives are Bashayer Almanwari in the 100m event and Tala Abu-Jubara, the first Qatari female rower at the Olympics.
The QOC campaign calls on the sporting community to get behind Team Qatar stars to make the nation proud.
QOC encourages followers on social media to show support via Instagram, Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, and Snapchat accounts.
Qatar's development in sport is built on a far-sighted vision, hard work, and commitment, with athletes inspiring future generations.

0-4789-12-t.subevent: From November 2018 to June 2019, South Korean courts awarded compensation from Japanese companies to forced wartime laborers, reopening long-standing tensions with Japan.

In July 2019, Japan removed South Korea from its 'white list' of preferential export treatment, citing alleged violations of UN prohibitions on exporting to North Korea and a breakdown of trust in export-control talks.

The removal exposed over 1,100 products to enhanced regulatory scrutiny, particularly three chemicals—hydrogen fluoride, fluorinated polyimide, and photoresists—critical to semiconductor manufacturing.
Market analysts warned that the trade dispute could reduce South Korean GDP by as much as 2.6% in 2020 due to the importance of the semiconductor sector.
SK Hynix began switching to domestic sourcing of hydrogen fluoride, and LG reportedly tested Taiwanese hydrogen fluoride as a replacement for Japanese product.
Japanese automotive exports to South Korea fell by 60 percent from April to September 2019, and Japan's share of South Korean beer imports dropped from 16 percent to 1.5 percent in 2019.
In mid-December 2019, senior Japanese and South Korean trade officials met for hours, reported reaching 'common ground,' and agreed to hold another dialogue in Seoul.
Japan has been approving recent export requests for the key chemicals on a timely basis, allaying concerns about disruption to South Korea's semiconductor industry.
In November 2019, U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo pressured South Korea to not withdraw from the GSOMIA intelligence-sharing agreement, which played a critical role in regional security.

9-21734-6-t.subevent: Amazon announced it would remove Parler from its cloud hosting service Amazon Web Services due to violent content and lack of moderation, effective Sunday at 11:59 PM Pacific time, making Parler's website and app inaccessible.
Parler CEO John Matze warned that the deplatforming could lead to service interruptions and said rebuilding from scratch could take up to a week.
Matze accused Amazon of trying to completely remove free speech off the internet.
Apple removed Parler from its app store, citing threats of violence and illegal activity and insufficient moderation, and suspended it until the issues are resolved.
Google had already dropped Parler from the Google Play Store on Friday.
Matze wrote that Apple was banning Parler until they give up free speech and accused Apple of being a software monopoly.
Matze promised to share details about next plans soon, saying they have many options.

1-15203-8-1.subevent: Firefighters battled nearly two dozen wildfires in California after a week of blazes burned over 1 million acres, killing five people, destroying over 1,000 structures, forcing thousands to flee, and affecting at least 23 counties, with two fires ranking as the second and third largest in state history and the total burned area equaling the size of Rhode Island.

Climate scientist Daniel Swain called the scope astonishing given the absence of strong offshore winds, as President Trump issued a major disaster declaration and the National Weather Service issued a red flag warning for more thunderstorms.

Experts said climate change is affecting California through hotter temperatures, less dependable precipitation, and earlier snowpack melt, with Swain noting that extreme heat dries out air and vegetation, leaving the state a tinderbox when lightning strikes hit, and that the amount burned last week exceeds the totals for 2018 and 2017.
The fires burned part of Big Basin Redwoods State Park, damaging historic buildings and infrastructure, though it was unknown whether redwood trees were engulfed.
Nearly all Cal Fire crews were in the field, some working 72-hour shifts, with over 13,000 fire personnel on scene and aid from other states, but Governor Gavin Newsom said it was not enough.

The fires began Aug. 15 when over 1,200 lightning strikes hit within 72 hours during some of the hottest temperatures ever recorded, including 130°F in Death Valley, with over 12,000 lightning strikes and 600 fires total that week.

Volunteers helped evacuate seniors and individuals with intellectual disabilities; hundreds lost homes, with quotes from Hank Hanson and Assemblywoman Cecilia Aguiar-Curry; the American Red Cross placed survivors in hotels or shelters with spacing due to the pandemic.

Sonoma County supervisor Susan Gorin, who lost her home in the 2017 Tubbs Fire and rebuilt, found ashes on her patio from a nearby fire, calling it the third major fire in four years; Swain and others published a study saying climate change doubled extreme-risk days, while scientist Jon Keeley argued the study failed to show temperature increase drives fires and cited fire suppression and fuel buildup, as President Trump accused California of failing to sweep its forests.
UCLA's Swain concluded that global warming is affecting fire size and speed, answering yes to whether the character of fires is changing.

10-6823-6-t.subevent: Users report that updating to iOS 10.1.1 causes iPhones to turn off when the battery falls below a certain percentage.
A thread on Apple's support forums grows to 13 pages with complaints about battery issues.
The original forum post describes the phone dying at 30% charge, and many others corroborate.
Hundreds of users complain on Twitter about their iPhones randomly shutting down.
Apple announces it will replace malfunctioning iPhone 6S batteries free of charge under certain circumstances.
The battery issue affects other iPhone models including Apple's latest.
Some users find that turning off the Raise to Wake feature helps, but not all users resolve the problem.

1-15293-1-3.subevent: A capsule containing the first significant quantities of rock from asteroid Ryugu parachuted down near Woomera in South Australia on Saturday evening (GMT) and was found by a recovery team lying on the sandy ground with its parachute draped over a bush.

The samples were originally collected by the Japanese spacecraft Hayabusa-2, which spent more than a year investigating Ryugu before returning to Earth and released the capsule as it approached Earth, firing its engines to push off in another direction.
The official Hayabusa-2 Twitter account reported that the capsule and its parachute had been found at 19:47 GMT.

Dr. Yuichi Tsuda said at a press conference that the capsule collection was perfectly done with no damage, and Dr. Hitoshi Kuninaka said they succeeded in sample return as planned and can move on to the next stage, including the MMX mission to Phobos.

Earlier on Saturday, the capsule was seen as a dazzling fireball over Australia's Coober Pedy region, deployed parachutes, and transmitted a beacon; after sunrise, the recovery team in a helicopter visually confirmed the capsule's location.
The capsule was taken to a quick-look facility for inspection, and Jaxa collected gases from inside for analysis, though it is not yet known if they come from the Ryugu sample.
Afterwards, the capsule will be airlifted to Japan and transported to a curation chamber at Jaxa in Sagamihara for analysis and storage.

Scientists said the samples would reveal information about the Solar System's history and the delivery of water and life ingredients to Earth, and researchers from Japan and other countries will study the material.
The Hayabusa-2 spacecraft, which bypassed Earth after releasing its capsule, is being sent on another mission to a smaller asteroid, expected to reach it in 2031.

18-10856-4-1.subevent: Fortnite's Battle Royale and Save the World modes share an in-game currency called V-Bucks, which can be earned in PvE but not in Battle Royale.
Some Battle Royale players farm V-Bucks in Save the World, causing frustration among PvE players who feel their mode is flooded with players not interested in cooperation.
Various guides and websites teach Battle Royale players how to farm V-Bucks in Save the World, though a player reports it is a grind earning about 3,000 V-Bucks per month.
Some Battle Royale players prefer to spend real money on V-Bucks rather than play Save the World, while others log into Save the World daily for V-Bucks and then switch to Battle Royale.
Some players admit their motivation for playing Save the World is earning V-Bucks for Battle Royale, and there are calls to separate the two modes with different currencies.
The shared V-Bucks economy may benefit Epic by encouraging Battle Royale players to purchase Save the World and keeping both modes active.
Epic Games declined to comment on plans for V-Bucks when Save the World goes free-to-play, as the community split is evident with separate subreddits and demands to split the modes.

Resentment exists because Battle Royale received primary focus while Save the World remained a paid early access, and there is fear that when Save the World becomes free, it will be used solely as a V-Bucks farming ground for Battle Royale.

12-wiki-img/8436-1/8436-1-3.subevent: The University of Manitoba uses Respondus anti-cheating software that records webcams and monitors facial detection, motion, and keyboard activity during remote exams, piloting it in summer and making it available for fall.
An ethicist and the students union raise concerns about the software's AI and webcam monitoring.

Student union president Jelynn Dela Cruz expresses concerns about data storage and access, says the union is in talks with administration, and notes that students worry about classmates watching them via alternative software.

U of M spokesperson Chris Rutkowski says the software underwent rigorous privacy evaluation, files are stored securely in the cloud and removed after the appeal period, and notes that students are watched by peers in classes.

Ethicist Neil McArthur says he will not use the software, calling it a clear violation of privacy and stating that consent is coerced; he plans to give take-home exams with 24-hour completion windows.

Other institutions have different approaches: University of Regina uses anti-cheating as a pilot; University of Winnipeg uses live proctoring on Zoom and plans to pilot invigilation software; Red River College does not use anti-cheating software but takes a proactive approach with education and multiple evaluations.
Respondus COO Jodi Feeney says the program is designed with student privacy; CEO David Smetters says proctoring flags do not automatically lead to penalties, giving an example of a door knock.

4-35540-1-2.subevent: Fighting between the Myanmar army and the Kachin Independence Army in Kachin State displaces thousands of civilians.
Local residents flee in at least three townships, with some pinned down by the fighting.
More than 150 people have been unable to leave an area of heavy fighting near Hpakant for a week.
Fortify Rights reports that the Myanmar government systematically prevents aid groups from visiting displaced areas.
UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator Knut Ostby condemns the violence and appeals for humanitarian access.
Government spokesperson Zaw Htay denies that the military is blocking aid to civilians.
A coalition of over 30 Kachin civil society groups publishes a letter urging the UN Security Council to refer the Myanmar army to the International Criminal Court for war crimes.
The peace process in Myanmar has stalled since the National League for Democracy came to power two years ago.
Analysts cite lack of trust and momentum, though ethnic armed groups continue efforts to discuss core peace issues.

1-15076-2-4.subevent: Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon rose more than 50% in the first three months of 2020 compared to the same period last year.
Brazil’s environmental agency scaled back enforcement measures during the COVID-19 pandemic, leaving the forest and indigenous tribes more vulnerable.
Indigenous leaders reported ongoing invasions by loggers and hunters and expressed fear that the virus could spread to isolated tribes.

Since taking office in 2019, President Jair Bolsonaro slashed funding and enforcement at FUNAI, the indigenous affairs agency, and appointed a federal police officer with agribusiness connections to head it.
In April 2020, FUNAI passed law IN 09, preventing indigenous lands awaiting demarcation from being labeled as indigenous in the land registry.
The Brazilian government considered making Provisional Measure MP 910 permanent, allowing those who illegally deforested before December 2018 to purchase protected lands at reduced prices.
Last summer, the Guajajara tribe's 'Guardians' conducted patrols to pursue illegal logging operations deep into the jungle.
Reports of illegal logging and violent attacks increased during the pandemic, including illegal gold mining in the Yanomami reserve and the first known COVID-19 death of a 15-year-old Yanomami boy.

Two indigenous leaders were killed: a 33-year-old leader of the Uru-eu-wau-wau reserve was assassinated on April 18, and Zezico Rodrigues Guajajara of the Guajajara tribe was killed by a shotgun-wielding assailant in March.

20-wiki-img/11947-1/11947-1-2.subevent: Hagia Sophia reopened for Friday prayers for the first time in 85 years, with thousands of people including top officials participating.
President Erdoğan stated that Hagia Sophia has returned to its original form as a mosque, and a Turkish court annulled the 1934 decree that had turned it into a museum.
By mid-Friday morning, congregants arrived with prayer rugs and Quran verses were read over loudspeakers, while police maintained security and worshippers wore face masks and sat spaced out.
Authorities stopped accepting new visitors around Hagia Sophia due to the crowd and pandemic.
Paintings, depictions, and mosaics were covered with curtains during prayers.
Erdoğan recited from the Quran inside the mosque, then Ali Erbaş delivered the Friday sermon with a sword, and four muezzins recited the adhan before the prayer began with Islamic rites.

The Diyanet will oversee religious services and the Culture Ministry will supervise restoration, with the site open to tourists free of charge, and the sword tradition will continue for Friday prayers.

11-23591-6-1.subevent: Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said Malaysia cannot accept same-sex marriage or LGBT rights.
Mahathir explained that some things are not acceptable even if seen as human rights in Western countries.
Two women were caned for 'attempting lesbian sex' in Terengganu.
Mahathir denounced the punishment, saying it 'did not reflect the justice or compassion of Islam'.
A gay bar in Kuala Lumpur was raided by police and religious enforcement officials.
A transgender woman was beaten up by a group of assailants in Seremban.
The minister in charge of Islamic affairs ordered the removal of portraits of two LGBT activists from an art exhibition.
Malaysia describes oral and anal sex as against the order of nature, with civil law stipulating jail, caning, and fines for offenders.

0-4819-1-2.subevent: At least six Vietnamese families fear their relatives are among the 39 bodies found in a lorry trailer in Essex.
Pham Thi Tra My, 26, sent texts saying she could not breathe and has not been heard from since.

A 48-year-old man is arrested at Stansted Airport, and two people from Warrington are held on suspicion of manslaughter and conspiracy to traffic people; the lorry driver is in custody on suspicion of murder.
People smugglers have returned money to some families.
Relatives of Nguyen Dinh Luong and a 19-year-old woman also fear their loved ones are among the victims.
The Vietnamese Embassy confirms contact with Essex police but no official identification yet.
Police initially said victims were all believed to be Chinese but now say the picture is developing; they urge anyone with information to come forward.
GPS data shows the trailer crossed between the UK and Europe in the days before it was found; it was leased from a rental company.
The UN International Organization for Migration says the discovery does not indicate a major shift in migration patterns.

0-4827-4-1.subevent: More than 100 wildfires have spread in various regions across Lebanon over the past 24 hours, including Chouf, Akkar, and Keserwan.
The fires are related to unusual high October temperatures exceeding 30 degrees Celsius, and observations show that such incidents are increasing due to climate change.
The most intense wildfires have been spreading in the Chouf area since the early hours of Monday, October 14.
The Mechref fire is seen as a serious threat due to its proximity to residential areas, schools, and the industrial area of Nehme.
Consequences include electricity cuts, residents fleeing, economic losses, health implications, and the death of Salim Abou Mjahed from smoke inhalation.
The fires also lead to contamination of soil and water and reduction of soil fertility.
These wildfires prove that Lebanon has a poor approach to disaster risk management, with no proactive measures and insufficient reactive measures.
Inhabitants are joining efforts with emergency services, and Cyprus is sending aircraft to help combat the fires.
The article calls for developing appropriate risk management plans, including risk assessments and strategies, citing France's municipal protection plans as an example.

28-43-2-3.subevent: The Dutch Coast Guard informed that at least 21 containers have washed ashore at the beaches of Vlieland, Terschelling and Ameland, adding that there are still containers in the water, and warned that interested parties should not help with cleaning activities as three unlocalized containers could contain hazardous materials.

Germany’s Central Command for Maritime Emergencies reported that some of the containers that went overboard have been spotted, including six in German waters, but it is yet to be determined whether a container with dangerous goods was among them.
MSC announced that it has started a clean-up operation in response to a substantial spill of containers in the North Sea.
MSC stated that a number of containers were damaged or lost overboard amid very difficult conditions.
MSC appointed a salvage company to coordinate the retrieval of cargo and beach clean-up operations and is deploying specialized ships equipped with sonar to search for missing cargo at sea.

MSC added that it takes this incident very seriously, both in terms of the impact on the natural environment and damage to customers’ cargo, and is collaborating with local authorities in all aspects of the clean-up.
MSC said that customers who seek further information will receive direct communications in the coming days and are invited to contact local MSC representatives.
MSC Zoe proceeded to Bremerhaven for cargo discharge operations and moored at 00:35 after being accompanied by the multipurpose vessel Neuwerk.
MSC said it was analyzing the causes of the incident.

4-35339-2-t.subevent: A crowd surge occurred around 9:15 p.m. during Travis Scott's Astroworld Festival set, causing panic and injuries as people fell and became unconscious.
Eight people died, including a 14-year-old and a 16-year-old, and only six families were notified.
Twenty-five people were taken to hospitals, with 13 still hospitalized Saturday, including a 10-year-old in critical condition, and over 300 were treated on-site.
About 50,000 people attended the festival, with 528 Houston police and 755 private security providing security.
Travis Scott expressed devastation in a tweet, saying his prayers go out to the families and he supports the Houston PD investigation.
The festival's second day on Saturday was canceled.
An NRG Park spokesperson said they were deeply saddened and cooperating with authorities.
A 16-year-old attendee described being trapped in a crowd pile for about 15 minutes, suffocating, and seeing bodies.
Alleighya Odom, 21, described the crowd force pushing her and seeing people on the ground crying for help.

6-19298-5-5.subevent: Kumbh Mela is the largest peaceful congregation of pilgrims on earth, during which participants bathe in a sacred river.
Devotees believe that bathing in the Ganges frees them from sins and liberates them from the cycle of birth and death.
Millions of people gather without invitation, including ascetics, saints, sadhus, aspirants (kalpavasis), and visitors.
The festival is held at Allahabad, Haridwar, Ujjain, and Nasik every four years by rotation and is attended by millions irrespective of caste, creed, or gender.
Primary bearers of the tradition belong to akhadas, ashrams, religious organizations, or are individuals living on alms.
Kumbh Mela plays a central spiritual role in the country, exerting a mesmeric influence on ordinary Indians.
The event encapsulates astronomy, astrology, spirituality, ritualistic traditions, and social and cultural customs and practices, making it extremely rich in knowledge.

Knowledge and skills related to Kumbh Mela are transmitted through ancient religious manuscripts, oral traditions, historical travelogues, texts by historians, and most importantly through teacher-student relationships in ashrams and akhadas.

7-36719-5-2.subevent: Malaysia arrested more than 4,000 people for violating lockdown orders, with police setting up roadblocks and inspections, and one man jumped into the Strait of Malacca to avoid arrest.
Senior minister Datuk Seri Ismail Sabri Yaakob announced that Malaysia entered a 'harsh mode' of the Movement Control Order to enforce isolation.

Other countries also enforced lockdowns: Florida charged a pastor for mass gatherings, Australia fined citizens gathering in groups, and the Philippines arrested over 20,000 violators after President Duterte said to shoot them if needed.
Malaysia reported that the lockdown decreased the spread of COVID-19, with 3,116 total cases and 50 deaths as of Friday.
Google data showed an 81% decrease in citizen presence at retail and recreation sites in Malaysia compared to a month earlier.
Authorities arrested people for allegedly spreading misinformation about the virus online, and journalists said they were self-censoring to avoid punishment.

Jason Kelley of the Electronic Frontier Foundation warned that human rights workers, free expression advocates, and activists are in danger from the government's curtailing of free expression beyond what is required.

Economists said political turmoil in Kuala Lumpur, stemming from Mahathir Mohamad's failed power consolidation in February and the return of the old ruling party, makes it hard for the government to fight the coronavirus.

The government announced the People's Economic Stimulus Package (PRIHATIN) worth $57.3 billion, including cash aid, loans, deferred taxes, and debt payments, which law firm partners described as far-reaching and encouraging.

12-8133-2-t.subevent: Brett Hall started using the Corona-Warn contact tracing app developed by the German government.
The app documents digital encounters between smartphones and informs users if they had contact with someone who tested positive, while keeping identities anonymous.

The International Digital Accountability Council (IDAC) analyzed 108 COVID-19 apps in 41 countries and found privacy concerns, including missing or inadequate privacy policies, permission requests that could pass data to third parties, and unencrypted transmissions.

The Healthy Together app in Utah asked for permission to read location and contacts, while North Dakota's CARE19 app was initially criticized for using Foursquare but later disclosed the arrangement with Foursquare agreeing not to retain data.
Matthew Guariglia of the Electronic Frontier Foundation warned that privacy agreements are not a guarantee and that storing sensitive data creates a security risk.
Researchers found most apps protect privacy well, with Private Kit and Pathcheck GPS being the most secure, and IDAC gave a preliminary thumbs up to Corona-Warn.
California is not using a contact tracing app, with the Department of Health stating that most tracing can be done by phone, text, email, and chat.
The developer of CARE19 explained that the app uses Foursquare for reverse geo-location to convert coordinates into business names without sharing or retaining data.
Apple and Google provided statements about their exposure notification technology, outlining privacy protections and conditions that apps must meet for government use.

14-9339-6-t.subevent: President Richard Nixon signed Title IX of the Education Amendment Act into law on June 23, 1972.
Bridgewater State athletic director John Harper commented on the increased opportunities for girls now compared to 30 to 40 years ago.

Title IX states that no person in the United States shall be excluded from participation in, denied benefits of, or subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving federal financial assistance on the basis of sex.
The Chronicle of Higher Education reported that nearly 200,000 female athletes competed on NCAA teams in 2012, compared to 31,852 in 1972.
Stonehill College vice president Paula Sullivan said Title IX was the impetus behind promoting athletics for girls and women and listed various benefits of sports participation.
Paula Sullivan lived athletic lives before and after Title IX, with a Hall of Fame playing career at Bridgewater State ending in 1971 and a coaching career at Stonehill beginning later that year.

Bentley University Hall of Famer Barbara Stevens recalled that change did not come easily and that in her high school days it was sometimes embarrassing to be known as a female athlete, but now kids embrace it.
Mary Lydon, a Bridgewater State alumna from the Class of 1955 who advocated for gender equity before Title IX, called the impact of Title IX mind-boggling.
Mary Pratt, a 93-year-old former All-American Girls Professional Baseball League pitcher and teacher/coach, said Title IX brought a far different approach and more opportunities for girls.

0-4504-1-2.subevent: Twelve-year-old Nefisa Nasser collects water from a street faucet as part of her daily routine.
Muhammed Nasser negotiates traffic fines and borrows money while his wife cooks lunch without running water or electricity.
Abdullah Alrahabi supplies water from his well and states that Yemenis are accustomed to managing without the state.
The Houthi militia has taken over the capital, southern separatists are fighting, and former President Saleh appears to be renewing his sway.
Experts and officials say that Saleh deliberately kept state institutions weak and created parallel security forces.
Moneef Almaqtari describes living in a hut and struggling with poverty, stating that the crisis worsens with each president.
Students at Sana University complain about favoritism and corruption, while a government employee admits to taking bribes due to unpaid salaries.
Yemenis are skeptical of Houthi promises of reform, and Mr. Nasser says the Houthis have done little for them.

5-5941-3-1.subevent: A U.N. report estimates that about a quarter of Venezuelans need humanitarian assistance, contradicting President Maduro's denial of a crisis.
The U.N. is caught in the political struggle between Maduro and opposition leader Guaido.
Venezuelan troops blocked U.S.-backed aid convoys from Colombia and Brazil, but Maduro accepted aid from Russia.
The report warns that politicization of aid makes delivery difficult.
The report uses a broad range of sources and calls for scaled-up humanitarian response in Venezuela.
The report estimates 94% of the population lives in poverty and over 3 million people have fled the country.
The report details millions in need of healthcare, water, food, and education, with resurgent diseases and children out of school.

1-14859-6-t.subevent: As of April 12, more than 6.8 million doses of the Johnson & Johnson vaccine have been administered in the U.S.

CDC and FDA are reviewing six reported U.S. cases of a rare and severe type of blood clot, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with low platelets, in women aged 18 to 48, with symptoms occurring 6 to 13 days after vaccination.
The treatment for this specific blood clot is different from typical treatment; heparin may be dangerous and alternative treatments are needed.
CDC will convene a meeting of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices on Wednesday to review the cases, and FDA will review that analysis as it also investigates these cases.

Until that process is complete, the agencies are recommending a pause in the use of the J&J vaccine out of an abundance of caution to ensure healthcare providers are aware and can plan for proper recognition and management.
The agencies state that these adverse events appear to be extremely rare and that COVID-19 vaccine safety is a top priority.
People who have received the J&J vaccine and develop severe headache, abdominal pain, leg pain, or shortness of breath within three weeks after vaccination should contact their healthcare provider.
Healthcare providers are asked to report adverse events to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System.
CDC and FDA will provide additional information and answer questions later today at a media briefing, with a recording available on the FDA’s YouTube channel.

0-4526-6-1.subevent: The Asian Football Confederation confirmed that 22 out of 24 teams have advanced to the AFC Asian Cup China 2023 Qualifiers Final Round.
13 teams, including host China PR and reigning champion Qatar, sealed their places for the AFC Asian Cup 2023 tournament after the conclusion of the Preliminary Joint Qualifiers Round 2.
The 22 teams in the Final Round consist of three lowest-ranked second-placed teams, all eight third and fourth-placed teams from Groups A to H, and three best fifth-placed teams.
The remaining four teams, ranked 36 to 39, will compete in the AFC Asian Cup China 2023 Qualifiers Play-offs over two legs on September 7 and October 12, 2021.
The draw for the Qualifiers Play-offs will be held on June 24, 2021.

24-32425-1-1.subevent: Pope Francis appoints Sr. Alessandra Smerilli as interim Secretary of the Dicastery for Promoting Integral Human Development and as a delegate of the Vatican Covid-19 Commission.
Sr. Smerilli replaces Msgr. Bruno Marie Duffé and Fr. Augusto Zampini, who have returned to their dioceses.
Sr. Smerilli has served as Undersecretary at the Dicastery since March 2021.
Pope Francis orders that the management team of the Vatican Covid-19 Commission be composed of Cardinal Turkson, Sr. Smerilli, and Fr. Fabio Baggio.
Sr. Smerilli expresses gratitude for the appointment and commits to serve with humility, passion, and a spirit of obedience.
Fr. Augusto Zampini announces his return to his diocese and expresses confidence in Sr. Smerilli's leadership.

2-34596-7-t.subevent: Lunar Prospector was a NASA Discovery Program mission designed to perform a low polar orbit investigation of the Moon.
The mission was launched on January 6, 1998, from Cape Canaveral using a Lockheed Martin LMLV2 rocket.

Beginning on January 15, 1998, Lunar Prospector spent one year mapping the entire surface of the Moon from about 100 kilometers, and the Neutron Spectrometer indicated significant amounts of water ice at the lunar poles.
The mission was extended for seven months starting in January 1999, with the orbit lowered to about 10 kilometers, obtaining higher resolution data.
At mission end, the spacecraft was deliberately crashed into a crater near the lunar south pole to confirm water ice, but no water was detected in the impact plume.
During the cruise phase, mid-course corrections, instrument boom deployment, and calibration occurred, and on arrival the spacecraft was placed into its nominal lunar polar orbit.
The spacecraft was shaped like a drum, made of epoxy graphite, with solar cells, batteries, and three radial booms, and had no onboard computer to reduce costs.
The mission successfully completed all objectives over 19 months, ending on July 31, 1999, with the spacecraft directed to crash into a crater near the south pole.

1-15910-2-1.subevent: Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin announced that self-isolation rules and travel permits would be waived from June 9, allowing all residents including the elderly and chronically ill to freely travel and visit public places.

Effective June 9, hairdressing salons, veterinary clinics, personnel recruitment agencies, NGOs, cemeteries, car sharing services, film and sound studios, and research centers reopened, while theaters, concert halls, and circuses were allowed to conduct rehearsals.

Starting June 16, dentist clinics, real estate, leasing, law, accounting, consulting, advertising, and market research businesses resumed normal activity, and sports competitions were allowed with no more than 10% seat occupancy, while summer cafes, libraries, museums, exhibition halls, and zoos reopened with visitor limits.
Starting June 23, gyms, fitness clubs, swimming pools, restaurants, cafes, canteens, bars, other catering outlets, spa salons, sunrooms, steam baths, and saunas were allowed to open.
All reopening organizations must comply with requirements of supervisory authorities and the consumer rights watchdog, and decisions on remaining restrictions were deferred.
Sobyanin stressed that residents must continue to follow self-protection rules, including wearing facemasks and maintaining social distancing of 1.5 meters, as the risk of infection remains.
The mayor's decree stated that dates for lifting restrictions may be changed depending on the epidemiological situation.
Moscow reported 197,018 total confirmed COVID-19 cases, with 2,001 new cases in the past 24 hours, 1,633 recoveries, 51 deaths (the lowest in two weeks), and 2,970 total deaths.

Moscow had declared a high alert on March 29, requiring self-isolation and closing many businesses, and began easing restrictions on May 12 with construction and on June 1 with public services and a walking schedule, while mask and glove mandates remained.

9-21751-1-1.subevent: Clashes broke out Sunday morning in three Israeli cities as police enforced lockdown restrictions in ultra-Orthodox communities.
In Jerusalem's Mea Shearim, hundreds clashed with police trying to shut down a yeshiva, shouting insults and throwing debris, leading to one arrest and water cannon use.

In Ashdod, police closed an ultra-Orthodox school, resulting in a confrontation where several dozen people injured four officers and damaged a fence, and police arrested four after protesters blocked traffic.
In Bnei Brak, clashes erupted as police shut down Vizhnitz Hasidic schools after the head rabbi initially ruled to open then backtracked.
Police stated they would continue to enforce virus restrictions in all communities.
Last week, a mob in Bnei Brak injured a police officer, leading to six arrests, and Prime Minister Netanyahu condemned the attack.

Health Minister Edelstein called for jailing lockdown violators, and Netanyahu and Edelstein appealed to Rabbi Kanievsky, who gave permission for some ultra-Orthodox schools to reopen if no confrontation with police.
The Health Ministry reported a decline in daily infections to 2,394 new cases, with total infections at 595,097 and deaths at 4,361.

6-18750-1-1.subevent: SpaceX launched a Falcon 9 rocket carrying a next-generation Dragon 2 cargo ship from Kennedy Space Center at 11:17 a.m. EST on December 6, after a one-day delay due to bad weather.
The Dragon 2 is the first cargo Dragon under a follow-on NASA contract and is designed to dock autonomously to the space station, unlike its predecessor.
The Falcon 9's first stage landed on a droneship in the Atlantic Ocean, marking SpaceX's 68th successful booster recovery.
The second stage deployed the Dragon 2 into orbit 12 minutes after launch, and the capsule is scheduled to dock at the Harmony module's upper port on Monday.
The Dragon 2 carries over 6,500 pounds of supplies, including crew supplies, science gear, spare parts, a commercial airlock known as Bishop Airlock, and other equipment.
The Bishop Airlock, developed by Nanoracks, is about five times larger than the Japanese experiment airlock and will be used to expose experiments to the vacuum of space.
Other cargo includes components for a new toilet, water recycling system, a nitrogen tank, and a rodent habitat with research specimens.
Experiments on board include studies of microgravity effects on heart and brain tissue, as well as the BioAsteroid experiment investigating microbial extraction of elements from asteroid material.
SpaceX holds NASA contracts for 20 resupply flights using the original Dragon and at least nine more using Dragon 2, plus a $2.6 billion contract for Crew Dragon.

0-4765-3-2.subevent: A plane carrying passengers from Juba crashed into Lake Yirol while attempting to land at Yirol Airport.
The crash killed 20 people, including Bishop Simon Adut Yuang of the Episcopal Church of South Sudan.
Thick fog around Yirol may have contributed to the accident.
Only three passengers survived: two children and an Italian doctor.
Other victims included a member of the Red Cross in South Sudan.
Regional government minister Abel Aguek commented that the weather was foggy and the plane crashed into the lake, and said the whole town was in shock with shops closed.
Local fishermen were first on the scene to rescue survivors and retrieve bodies.
Archbishop Justin Badi Arama expressed sadness over the crash and offered prayers for those involved.
Bishop Simon had succeeded Bishop Daniel Deng Abeil, was elected in May 2015, consecrated and enthroned that July, and leaves behind a wife and six children.

1-16234-1-1.subevent: President Obama announced new actions to reduce gun violence, including increased funding for mental health treatment and enhanced background checks.

Mental health advocates say media reports of mass shootings reinforce the impression that severe mental illness leads to violence, but studies show most people with severe mental illness are not violent.
People with serious mental illness account for about 4% of firearm homicides, while suicides constituted 61% of gun deaths in 2014.
Jeffrey Swanson says gun violence and mental illness have very little overlap and fixing the mental health system is not a silver bullet for reducing gun violence.
Mental health stakeholders are concerned about reinforcing the false association between mental illness and violence and call for criteria based on dangerous behavior rather than diagnosis alone.
Obama proposed a $500 million investment in mental health access, but some criticized including mental health reform in gun violence reduction orders.
Swanson supports comprehensive background checks with criteria based on risk indicators like violent assault convictions, restraining orders, and multiple DUIs, not just mental health history.
Studies found that a handgun ban in D.C. reduced gun suicides, Connecticut's permit-to-purchase law lowered gun suicide rates by 15%, and Missouri's repeal raised them by 16%.

Researchers monitor gun violence restraining orders, and Swanson notes that mass shooters like Jared Loughner and James Holmes had never been involuntarily committed and could legally purchase firearms.

27-33406-1-t.subevent: Authorities announced that Notre-Dame cathedral is ready to undergo restoration work more than two years after the blaze and remains on course to reopen in 2024.
The fire on April 15, 2019, destroyed the spire and much of the roof.
The focus until now had been on making the cathedral safe, including removing 40,000 pieces of damaged scaffolding.
Jean-Louis Georgelin stated that the cathedral stands solid on its pillars and its walls are solid.
Georgelin said they are determined to reopen the cathedral in 2024 and that it will be France's honour.
Authorities aim to celebrate the first full service on April 16, 2024, despite delays caused by the pandemic and lead spread.
Authorities will call for tenders to select companies for restoration work.
The cathedral's interior walls and floors will undergo a thorough cleaning process later this month.
The Grand Organ is being restored, with its 8,000 pipes dismantled and sent to organ builders across France, expected to be reassembled in October 2023.

6-19428-8-t.subevent: In the 1980s, the Shia school of thought spread rapidly in Ghana due to Lebanese Shia migration.
Shia Muslims in Ghana number about one million and are scattered across areas including Okra, Tamaleey, Kowmasey, and Owfaseey, where the entire population converted to Shia Islam.
Islamic centres and mosques for Ahlulbayt exist in Ghana, and Shia activities include teaching youth, commemorating Imams, and publishing magazines like al-Kawthar.
The roots of Shia Islam in Tunisia date to before the Fatimid empire, and the Berber people played a role during the martyrdom of Imam Hussain.
Shia belief spread in Tunisia during the 1950s and 1970s after Tijani al-Samawi left for Iraq.
Today Shia are found in many Tunisian cities, and their activities include celebrations, publications, and studying in Iran and Syria.
Islam reached Brazil through African worshipers and Ottoman immigrants, and Portuguese colonisation helped stabilize Muslims.
In the late 1950s, Brazil learned about Islam through businessmen; the first mosque was built in 1950 in Sao Paulo, and now there are over 60 Islamic centres and 40 mosques.
Shia Islam in Brazil increased due to mass Lebanese immigration in the first half of the 20th century, and the Shia population is about one million, 40% of Muslims.
Shia in Brazil have their own mosques and the Imam Khomeini Centre; they engage in funding establishments, publishing books, and now enjoy respect and exchange visits with Sunnis.

28-441-1-t.subevent: A bug in Apple's FaceTime software was discovered that lets users listen in on the people they are calling and even see through their front-facing camera without the recipient picking up the call.
The bug was flagged by 9to5Mac on Monday and quickly recreated by people across social media; CNN Business confirmed the bug multiple times in its own tests.
Apple said in a statement Monday night that it has identified a fix and will release a software update later this week, and it has started disabling the Group FaceTime feature for all users.
The bug affects iPhones and iPads running iOS 12.1 and Macs running macOS Mojave that have the Group FaceTime feature.

When activated, the caller hears live audio from the recipient's phone even though the recipient has not accepted the call, and the recipient's screen gives no indication that their conversation is being transmitted.
In some cases, the bug can also show live video of the recipient if they press a volume button to dismiss the call.
CNN senior editor Brian Ries successfully used the bug on friends, family members and a colleague, and in one instance was able to see video of the people he was calling.

To avoid the bug, users should disable FaceTime on all devices until Apple's software updates are released, by toggling off FaceTime in Settings on iPhone/iPad or selecting 'Turn FaceTime Off' in the FaceTime app on Mac.

1-14811-2-1.subevent: Spain becomes the first western European country to record over 500,000 Covid cases amid a surge as millions of children begin returning to school.
Spain logs 49,716 new cases and 237 deaths in the past week, with about a third of cases and deaths in Madrid, and has the fastest rise in daily confirmed cases in Europe since July.

The UK reports 349,500 cases, France 347,268, and Italy 277,634; a UK government source says there is significant concern the UK is 'six weeks behind France', and UK health secretary Matt Hancock describes the recent rises as concerning.

At the pandemic's peak on 31 March, Spain recorded 9,222 new cases and 849 deaths in a single day; in Madrid hospitals, 18% of beds are occupied by Covid patients compared with a national average of 7%.

Fernando Simón acknowledges the rise but notes 50% of new cases are asymptomatic and more than half are in people under 40; surgeon Ángela Hernández Puente warns that the hard-won gains of lockdown are being squandered by irresponsible behaviour and lack of proper preparations.

Professor Ildefonso Hernández-Aguado says there is no simple explanation for Spain's surge, but some regions failed to invest in contact tracing; Rafael Bengoa warns that micro-lockdowns will probably be required due to weak public health infrastructure.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez reassures parents about school reopening, while Madrid's regional president warns that almost all children returning to school are likely to pick up the virus; Madrid bans gatherings of more than 10 people and nearly doubles contact tracers.

France's Prof Antoine Fontanet warns of a critical situation in December if cases continue rising; the UK reports nearly 3,000 new cases in a day, a 50% increase and the highest since May, and experts warn that the risk of following Spain remains high and deaths may increase.

1-15160-1-2.subevent: Shakespeare's Globe Theatre called for urgent funding to avoid insolvency due to the devastating impact of the coronavirus pandemic.
The London venue has been shut since 20 March and warned MPs it is critically vulnerable and at risk of closure.
The Globe said it needs at least £5m to get back up and running and is ineligible for Arts Council England's relief, leaving it without emergency support.

In evidence to a select committee, the Globe stated it will become insolvent without emergency funding and continuation of the job retention scheme, calling the situation financially devastating and possibly terminal.
Conservative MP Julian Knight wrote to Culture Secretary Oliver Dowden calling the potential closure a tragedy and calling the Globe a world-renowned institution and national treasure.

The Globe raises 95% of its revenue through ticket sales, tours, education, retail, and catering, all dependent on being open, and warned this is the biggest threat to its future since opening in 1997.

The Globe argued it is a model for the non-subsidised arts sector that is well-run but has no mechanism to help it in such a crisis, and that it contributes to UK cultural life and stewards an important building.

Arts Council England said it received over 13,500 applications and could not help everyone, while the government claimed it is providing unprecedented support; the Theatres Trust anticipates significant theatre closures and Nuffield Southampton Theatres has gone into administration.

1-14830-1-1.subevent: Early in its formation, Jupiter moved closer to and then away from the sun due to interactions with the protoplanetary disc and other giant planets, and this movement affected Venus.
Observations of other planetary systems have shown that similar giant planet migrations soon after formation may be relatively common.
UCR astrobiologist Stephen Kane said that Jupiter's movement likely triggered Venus onto a path toward its current, inhospitable state.
Kane created a model that simulated the solar system, calculating the positions of all planets and how they pull on each other.
The model showed that when Jupiter was likely closer to the sun about a billion years ago, Venus likely had an orbital eccentricity of 0.3 and was more likely habitable.
As Jupiter migrated, Venus underwent dramatic climate changes, heating up and cooling off, increasingly losing its water into the atmosphere.
Scientists discovered the gas phosphine in Venus's clouds, which is typically produced by microbes and may indicate the presence of life, but Kane notes other processes could produce it.
Kane emphasized that it is important to understand what happened to Venus to gain insight into Earth's habitability.

21-30964-3-1.subevent: ISSF confirmed that the IOC officially approved quota qualification rules for shooting events at Tokyo 2020.
ISSF agreed to change regulations to reflect gender equality at an Executive Committee meeting in November.
The IOC gave the green light to the alterations, with 180 men and 180 women due to compete in three mixed team events and six men’s and six women’s individual competitions.
Quota place allocation will start from the 2018 ISSF World Championships in Changwon, where 48 individual and 12 mixed team Olympic quotas will be assigned.

The Tokyo 2020 shooting event programme has been a contentious issue within the ISSF in recent years.

The changes led to criticism from ISSF vice-president Luciano Rossi, with some members claiming he opposed them to help his potential bid for the ISSF Presidency.

2-34912-7-t.subevent: A new book reveals unprecedented details about Emperor Akihito's spending of public money and his royal staff.

33-2677-2-t.subevent: The book is a dictionary of slang used by hackers, different from technical jargon.
It explains that slang is used for fun and often derived from jargon.
The book is a revised version of the 'jargon file' maintained by hackers at several universities.
Guy Steele coordinated the revision, with contributions from five others and many hackers.
This edition adds pronunciation keys, cross-references, and explanatory notes.
As a teenager, Guy Steele visited the MIT computer lab and saw a PDP-6 computer playing chess and music.
He played a color version of Space War on a large screen.
In November 1968, he discovered his school had an IBM 1130 computer locked in the basement.
He obtained a computer manual and spent Thanksgiving vacation reading it, becoming hooked on programming.
He joined a small community of IBM 1130 hackers who maintained the computer and tutored students.
The dictionary defines 'FOO' and 'BAR' as common metasyntactic variable names used by hackers.
It defines 'BARF' as an interjection of disgust or a verb meaning to fail due to unacceptable input.
It defines 'BAZ' as the third metasyntactic variable after FOO and BAR, also a term of mild annoyance.
It defines 'BELLS AND WHISTLES' as unnecessary but often useful features of a program or object.
It defines 'BIGNUM' as a multiple-precision representation for very large integers or any very large number.

13-24525-1-t.subevent: Plans and proposals for blessings of unions of persons of the same sex are being advanced in some ecclesial contexts.
The Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith issued a Responsum ad dubium regarding the blessing of same-sex unions.
The Congregation explained that blessings are sacramentals that must be objectively ordered to receive grace according to God's designs.
It declared that it is not licit to impart a blessing on same-sex unions because they are not ordered to the Creator's plan and would constitute an imitation of the nuptial blessing.
The Congregation clarified that this declaration is not a form of unjust discrimination but a reminder of the truth of the liturgical rite.
It distinguished between blessing individual persons with homosexual inclinations (permitted) and blessing their unions (illicit).
The Church does not have the power to bless same-sex unions.
Pope Francis gave his assent to the publication of the Responsum ad dubium with the Explanatory Note.
The Responsum was signed by Prefect Cardinal Ladaria and Secretary Archbishop Morandi on February 22, 2021.

12-9074-9-t.subevent: Auckland butcher Shafeel Khan was visited by police and told to close because butchers are non-essential during the lockdown, despite earlier telling his customers not to stock up.

Imraan Ali highlights the importance of accessing halal meat ahead of Ramadan starting April 23, noting he has never purchased meat from supermarkets in 25 years.
The Federation of Islamic Associations of New Zealand states that only fish from New Zealand supermarkets is halal for devout Muslims and outlines the rules for halal slaughter.
Wellington butcher Shaimud Khan reopened his halal butchery for phone orders due to overwhelming demand, but will close if visited by police.
The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment says it is looking into halal butcheries and that essential services requirements may change.
Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern urges small businesses like butchers to close to prevent transmission of COVID-19.

0-4763-1.subevent: More than 50 other countries barred flights by Boeing's 737 Max aircraft before the FAA acted.

Trump witnessed a deal for Vietnamese airlines to buy Boeing jets including 100 737 Max models.

0-4841-2-1.subevent: The billionaire owners of the Daily Telegraph and the Sunday Telegraph are to put both titles up for sale and are reviewing all of their key assets, including the Telegraph Media Group.

0-4411-1-t.subevent: Russian Deputy Prime Minister Yuri Borisov met Venezuela's President Nicolas Maduro on Saturday to underline Moscow's support.

18-10690-5-t.subevent: The European Union's top court ruled in favor of a Romanian gay man's right to have his US husband live with him in Romania.
The European Court of Justice said the term 'spouse' is gender neutral.
Adrian Coman and his American partner Clai Hamilton were married in Brussels in 2010.

The ECJ ruled that member states must recognize gay marriages contracted in fellow EU states and grant same-sex couples the same residency rights.
The Romanian authorities refused a residence permit for Mr. Hamilton, citing Romanian legislation prohibiting same-sex marriage.

Romania's constitutional court referred the case to the ECJ.

1-wiki-img/15339-5/15339-5-1.subevent: Pope Francis and Benedict XVI both received their second dose of the COVID-19 vaccine.

Vatican residents, employees, and their families are receiving the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine in the Paul VI Hall.
Vatican City State has a population of about 800, with over 4,000 employees.
Vatican journalists accompanying Pope Francis on his trip to Iraq are required to get the COVID-19 vaccination.
Two Vatican cardinals published a statement urging equitable vaccine access for the Global South.

6-19298-5-7.subevent: Kumbh Mela is the largest peaceful congregation of pilgrims where they bathe in a sacred river, believed to free from sins and the cycle of birth and death.
Millions of people attend without invitation, including ascetics, saints, sadhus, aspirants, and visitors.
The festival is held in Allahabad, Haridwar, Ujjain, and Nasik every four years by rotation, attended by millions regardless of caste, creed, or gender.
Its primary bearers belong to akhadas, ashrams, religious organizations, or are individuals living on alms.

Kumbh Mela plays a central spiritual role, exerting a mesmeric influence on ordinary Indians, and encapsulates astronomy, astrology, spirituality, ritualistic traditions, and social and cultural customs.
Held in four cities, it involves different social and cultural activities, making it a culturally diverse festival.

Knowledge and skills related to the tradition are transmitted through ancient manuscripts, oral traditions, historical travelogues, texts produced by historians, and especially through the teacher-student relationship of sadhus in ashrams and akhadas.

12-8952-1-3.subevent: Pope Francis held the special Urbi et Orbi blessing on Friday from the steps of St. Peter's Basilica.
The extraordinary blessing was held due to the gravity of the global Covid-19 situation, with more than half the world's population confined to their homes.
Standing in a deserted St. Peter's Square, Pope Francis spoke to the world through Facebook, YouTube, TV, and radio.
He prayed in the presence of the ancient icon of Mary Salus Populi Romani and the miraculous crucifix from the church of San Marcello.
The Pope exposed the Blessed Sacrament for adoration and imparted his Apostolic Blessing, offering a plenary indulgence.
Pope Francis offered a meditation on the Gospel of Mark (4:35-41), reflecting on the evening darkness and the disciples' fear.
He said the pandemic reminds us we are all in the same boat and exposes our vulnerability and false certainties.
He called on people to seize the time of trial as a time of choosing what matters, and highlighted the example of those who have given their lives.
He concluded by entrusting everyone to the Lord through the intercession of Mary, and gave a blessing.

0-4398-1-1.subevent: Ecuador's government declared a state of emergency after protesters opposed to a fuel price hike disrupted transport nationwide.

Some protesters clashed with police, who fired tear gas to disperse crowds; Interior Minister Maria Paula Romo said 19 people had been arrested.
Some protesters burned tyres and threw objects at armoured police vans, drawing criticism from President Moreno, who said he would not allow them to 'impose chaos'.
Under the emergency measure, Moreno's government can restrict freedoms and deploy the armed forces to maintain order.

The elimination of fuel subsidies is part of Moreno's plan to shore up Ecuador's economy and ease its debt burden; the government agreed to cut public spending as part of an IMF loan deal, and Ecuador announced it was leaving OPEC to raise revenue.

2-34985-6-1.subevent: Politicians, economists, and some scientists have assumed climate tipping points are low probability, but evidence mounts that they are more likely, have high impacts, and are interconnected.
The IPCC introduced tipping points two decades ago, considering them likely only above 5°C warming, but recent special reports suggest they could be exceeded between 1 and 2°C of warming.
Current national pledges could lead to at least 3°C warming, but cost-benefit analyses assuming more likely tipping points align with IPCC recommendations to limit warming to 1.5°C.

Research shows the Amundsen Sea embayment of West Antarctica might have passed a tipping point, with irreversible grounding line retreat, potentially leading to 3 meters of sea-level rise and destabilizing the rest of the ice sheet.

The Greenland ice sheet is melting at an accelerating rate and could add 7 meters to sea level over thousands of years if it passes a threshold, possibly doomed at 1.5°C of warming, which could occur by 2030.

Other tipping points could be triggered at low warming levels, including Arctic sea ice loss with a 10-35% chance of being nearly ice-free in summer at 2°C warming, and mass coral bleaching with 99% of tropical corals projected to be lost at 2°C warming.
Deforestation and climate change destabilize the Amazon rainforest, with estimates of a tipping point between 20% and 40% forest-cover loss; about 17% has been lost since 1970.
Earth system models are starting to include biogeochemical feedbacks that increase climate sensitivity, hinting that a global tipping point is possible.
The article concludes that evidence from tipping points suggests a state of planetary emergency requiring urgent action, as the intervention time left to prevent tipping may have shrunk.

9-21834-8-2.subevent: President Trump declared Sunday a National Day of Prayer after designating a national emergency.
Megachurches streamed their Sunday service online, and Trump tweeted that he was watching a service by Pastor Jentezen Franklin.

Greg Laurie's Harvest Fellowship had over 230,000 online attendees and more than 1,400 people commit online to follow Jesus.

Catholic bishops in Pennsylvania and Ohio dispensed with the requirement to attend Mass, and the Mormon Church halted all worship services worldwide.

3-17274-6-t.subevent: Deadly clashes erupted between Moroccan forces and local rebels in Western Sahara.

Morocco annexed Western Sahara in the mid-1970s after Spain withdrew, leading to guerrilla warfare until a U.N.-brokered cease-fire in 1991.

1-14897-1-4.subevent: Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon rose more than 50% in the first three months of 2020 compared to the same period in 2019.

Brazil's environmental agency scaled back enforcement measures during the COVID-19 pandemic, increasing the vulnerability of the forest and indigenous tribes.

Turkey and Russia agreed in September 2018 to turn Idlib into a de-escalation zone, but the regime intensified its attacks starting on April 26.
